record.what: In 2014-2015, two additional scanning projects at Hawara used satellite-based methods.
record.context: Prevented from conducting physical excavations, researchers turned to spaceborne technology to probe the site beneath the surface. These non-invasive efforts aimed to map the subterranean layout without disturbing the ground above, bypassing site access restrictions. The resulting datasets provided fresh digital evidence that reinvigorated claims regarding the lost labyrinth.

record.what: The 2015 Merlin Burrows satellite work revealed layered structures, a central atrium, and a symbolic 'Omega moat' or Shen ring-like boundary.
record.context: The imagery provided geometric evidence that proponents claimed matched ancient descriptions of a vast, structured underground complex. By identifying specific features like an atrium and a symbolic perimeter, the scan results gave fresh momentum to alternative archaeological theories. It also framed satellite imaging as a primary tool for mapping sealed ancient sites.

record.what: The author previously wrote pieces titled 'The Real Labyrinth Scans You Missed' and 'Labyrinth of Hawara Revisited: The 2015 Satellite Scans' on AncientHistoryX.
record.context: These digital publications established the foundational context and detailed breakdown of the remote sensing data for an online audience interested in alternative history. By documenting the scan results prior to broader media pickup, the posts created a reference point for ongoing debate regarding the site's hidden features. This background laid the groundwork for analyzing later, more sensational claims.

record.what: On April 15, 2015, Zahi Hawass participated in a debate with Graham Hancock, author of 'Fingerprints of the Gods,' which popularized Gobekli Tepe.
record.context: The public confrontation highlighted the deep rift between established Egyptology and alternative history theorists regarding early human civilization. By bringing mainstream academic authority face-to-face with popular fringe theories, the event drew significant public attention to non-traditional archaeological sites. It signaled a turning point in how alternative claims were debated in popular media.

record.what: On July 21, 2015, a private meeting at the Crown Hotel in Harrogate, England featured Tim Akers, a former RAF officer and satellite expert, presenting synthetic aperture radar scans of Hawara.
record.context: The closed-door presentation unveiled non-public digital imagery to select researchers, bypasssing traditional academic publishing channels. By introducing military-grade radar technology to the site's analysis, the meeting galvanized independent efforts to prove the existence of deep subterranean chambers. This event solidified satellite radar as the centerpiece for modern fringe claims about Hawara.

record.what: Researchers Corrado Malanga, the SAR researcher, and Filippo Biondi published a paper and book in 2022 about using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) to explore the Giza pyramid.
record.context: The publication introduced advanced radar signal processing to mainstream audiences as a potential tool for detecting hidden subterranean features within ancient structures. It provided a technical reference point that alternative history proponents frequently cited to validate underground mapping claims. However, it also sparked immediate skepticism from academic institutions regarding methodology and data interpretation.

record.what: The 2022 SAR research on the Giza pyramid has not been peer-reviewed or corroborated by credible archaeologists.
record.context: The lack of formal peer review left the study's radical findings unsupported by independent experts in traditional Egyptology and geophysics. Without validation from academic credentials or on-the-ground excavation, the paper was dismissed by mainstream science. This critical void allowed the study to be adopted primarily by alternative history circles without rigorous oversight.

record.what: The claim appears to be a spin on questionable research conducted in 2022, later embellished by right-wing content creators including Infowars contributor Greg Reese, who publishes The Reese Report.
record.context: Unverified radar data migrated from specialized technical papers into mainstream fringe media, where it was recast as definitive proof of suppressed history. Media figures amplified the uncorroborated claims to fuel sensational narratives about ancient technology and hidden historical truths. This transformation demonstrates how speculative research can be weaponized within modern online information ecosystems.

record.what: Dr. Carmen Boulter passed away in 2022.
record.context: Her passing marked the end of an influential career dedicated to promoting alternative theories regarding ancient Egyptian technology and hidden subterranean structures. It left her extensive research, media appearances, and theoretical work to be carried forward by collaborators and followers in the fringe history community. Her legacy remains a touchstone for those questioning conventional archaeological narratives.

record.what: Carlotto's 2023 Sentinel-1 SAR study added shallow rectangular features that align with earlier findings.
record.context: By utilizing independent satellite radar data, the study offered partial corroboration for the geometric anomalies reported in earlier remote sensing attempts. The identification of these shallow formations helped refine the search area for potential subsurface features. It provided new technical material for analysts attempting to reconstruct the site's hidden layout.

record.what: Dunn published a 2024 follow-up book alleging connections between Nikola Tesla's research and the purported 'Giza Power Plant,' claims that remain unsubstantiated by credible sources.
record.context: The publication expanded upon fringe concepts connecting ancient monuments to advanced electromagnetic power generation, building on speculative interpretations of Egyptian engineering. By tying historic scientific figures to unverified archaeological theories, the work sought to modernize alternative historical narratives. Mainstream academics dismissed the publication due to a complete lack of physical or documentary evidence.

record.what: A May 2024 article in Smithsonian Magazine reported an 'anomaly' discovered near the Khafre pyramid area by researchers from Higashi Nippon International University, Tohoku University in Japan, and the National Research Institute of Astronomy and Geophysics in Egypt.
record.context: The joint international publication confirmed the presence of actual subterranean geological or structural variations using ground-based geophysical surveys. By documenting these features near iconic monuments, the legitimate study drew widespread media coverage. However, this coverage was quickly co-opted and exaggerated by online commentators to support far more radical claims.

record.what: The May 2024 research team used non-intrusive imaging technologies similar to the SAR described in the false claims, but the structures found do not match the description in the false claim.
record.context: While legitimate scientists used standard ground-penetrating radar to identify modest subterranean features, internet narratives altered the findings into discoveries of grand ancient machines or massive halls. This distinction highlights how actual scientific data is frequently distorted to fit pre-existing fringe theories. The actual findings were significant to geology, not alternative history.

record.what: The researchers in the May 2024 study described the anomaly as a combination of a shallow structure connected to a deeper structure.
record.context: This dual-layer spatial arrangement suggested a deliberate structural layout rather than a simple natural void beneath the surface. Identifying a shallow component linked to a deeper section gave archaeologists a specific target for investigating potential ancient construction or burial shafts. It established a clear physical framework for future localized studies.

record.what: The shallow structure identified in the May 2024 study is L-shaped and was filled in with sand after construction, possibly serving as an entrance to the deeper structure.
record.context: The deliberate backfilling with sand pointed to ancient efforts to seal, conceal, or structurally support the passage leading to the lower level. Understanding this feature helped explain why standard visual or surface surveys had missed the entrance for centuries. It offered a plausible archaeological function for the shallow portion of the anomaly.

record.what: The researchers in the May 2024 study are unsure of the deeper structure's contents, suggesting it could be empty or filled with materials such as sand and gravel.
record.context: The team maintained scientific rigor by refusing to speculate on unexcavated spaces, noting that natural sediment accumulation could easily account for the radar signals. This cautious stance directly contrasted with sensational online claims asserting the discovery of massive chambers or technology. It highlighted the standard gap between cautious academic reporting and popular speculation.

record.what: In 2024, scientists from the University of North Carolina Wilmington uncovered a long-buried branch of the Nile River that once flowed alongside the Giza pyramids.
record.context: The geographical discovery provided a clear explanation for how ancient builders transported massive stone blocks to the pyramid construction sites. By mapping the dried waterway, researchers solved a long-standing logistical mystery surrounding the construction of the Giza complex. The finding demonstrated how natural landscape changes over millennia shape historical understanding.

record.what: Dr. Abbas and his team released an additional report in 2024 with updated information about water levels at Hawara.
record.context: The updated hydrological data offered critical insights into the rising groundwater levels threatening the structural stability of the site's buried ruins. By documenting these environmental changes, the report provided practical information necessary for preserving the area's subterranean archaeological features. It also served to clarify what current imaging systems were detecting beneath the surface.

record.what: Claims that researchers discovered previously unknown structures beneath the Pyramid of Khafre using radar technology circulated online in March 2025.
record.context: Viral posts repackaged legitimate 2024 geophysical survey results into sensationalized tales of massive, secret underground cities. This wave of digital misinformation demonstrated how quickly complex scientific reports can be distorted across social platforms. It ultimately forced researchers to publicly clarify the modest, actual scale of their findings.

record.what: In a video posted on Feb. 7, 2025, Ciccolo claimed an event would occur at the Hotel Castello Artemide Congressi in Bologna, Italy, on March 15, 2025, where the Khafre Project would reveal recent discoveries and share a press release.
record.context: This announcement set the stage for public expectations surrounding the research team's upcoming disclosures. By naming a specific date and venue, it signaled a shift from private research to public presentation. The planned release generated anticipation within the community following the project's work.

record.what: On March 23, 2025, Ciccolo posted a video of researchers supposedly discussing their findings from the event.
record.context: The footage served as the first post-event material offered to the public to validate the gathering. It provided a visual record of the academics detailing their work, bridging the gap between the live conference and online followers. This release established a narrative of academic collaboration and confirmed that the announced proceedings had taken place.

record.what: On 23 March, 2025, Biondi and Malanga announced findings from the Khafre Project claiming the existence of a vast underground city beneath the Giza pyramids.
record.context: This statement marked one of the most extraordinary claims regarding the Giza Plateau's subterranean landscape. By putting their names to the assertion, the researchers dramatically escalated the stakes of the ongoing debate. The news altered public perception of the project, framing it around the discovery of a massive lost civilization site.

record.what: In 2025, Louis De Cordier released another major disclosure about the Hawara site.
record.context: This update built upon earlier controversies and discoveries surrounding the location. It reopened public and academic focus on the site's potential hidden features after years of speculation. The release forced mainstream authorities and independent researchers to re-examine existing data regarding the area.

record.what: In 2025, SAR scans of the Giza Plateau were released by the Khafre Research Project showing structures over a kilometer in scale.
record.context: The deployment of Synthetic Aperture Radar technology provided high-tech imagery to support earlier theoretical assertions. Releasing these images gave the team tangible evidence to present to both critics and supporters. It transformed theoretical claims about sub-surface anomalies into a debate over scientific data interpretation.

record.what: Akers and his team kept their findings secret for a decade, having learned from De Cordier's blacklisting, and finally released the data in 2025 without obtaining an excavation permit.
record.context: The prolonged silence was a direct strategy to avoid official suppression and academic exclusion. By bypassing the traditional authorization process, the team prioritized public dissemination over official sanction. This unauthorized publication forced the findings into the open, preventing authorities from quietly shelving the research.

record.what: Permission for the excavation was granted earlier in 2026.
record.context: Securing official approval shifted the effort from clandestine research to a sanctioned archaeological endeavor. This change eliminated the threat of legal interference and blacklisting for the involved parties. It established a legitimate framework that allowed heavy equipment and larger teams to operate openly on the site.

record.what: The 2026 dig is described as Egyptian-led, transparent, and focused on preservation alongside discovery.
record.context: Emphasizing local oversight and open methodologies was intended to counter past criticisms of foreign exploitation and secrecy. Prioritizing site integrity alongside excavation aimed to secure long-term support from international bodies. This operational shift redefined the project's public image from a sensationalist hunt to a responsible scientific survey.

record.what: On May 7, 2026, Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, through the Fayoum Antiquities Area, confirmed the launch of new fieldwork at Hawara.
record.context: Official acknowledgement by state authorities validated the site's ongoing importance and the legitimacy of the new efforts. It signaled a cooperative stance between administrative bodies and field archaeologists. This public endorsement paved the way for open reporting and official oversight of all subsequent discoveries.

record.what: The Archaeological Rescue Foundation released a document outlining a master plan for a new Hawara Rescue Project starting in early 2026.
record.context: The document established a structured framework aimed at preventing further site degradation while pursuing research goals. It signaled a shift toward organized, long-term operational planning rather than sporadic surveys. Providing a blueprint helped secure necessary institutional backing and public trust before physical work commenced.

record.what: On May 7, 2026 (Update #1), excavations at the Hawara Labyrinth began, and an article covered the dig with photos of a megalithic stone wall unearthed in the center of the Labyrinth area.
record.context: The immediate photographic evidence of massive stonework provided instant physical verification of the site's structural potential. This initial success vindicated years of preliminary radar surveys and non-invasive testing. The publication of the images energized international coverage and set a high-stakes tone for the rest of the field season.

record.what: Dr. Filippo Biondi of the Khafre Research Project agreed to scan Hawara once his Giza work is complete, estimated by Summer 2026, making it the fifth scanning project at Hawara.
record.context: Expanding the application of successful scanning techniques from Giza to Hawara brought cross-site analytical consistency. It established a clear timeline for the next major phase of non-invasive exploration. Committing to a fifth scan underscored the ongoing scientific dispute over the subterranean nature of the location.

record.what: The document release of the Hawara Rescue Project mission plan was permitted as of February 9, 2026.
record.context: Formal authorization to distribute the project's strategy cleared the way for public and institutional scrutiny. It ensured that the project's operational and conservation protocols were made transparent ahead of ground operations. This procedural clearance was a critical step in establishing the organizational legitimacy of the upcoming field season.

files.title: Ancient accounts of the Labyrinth
files.body:
The Labyrinth of Egypt was written about extensively by ancient authors. The guest on the Joe Rogan Experience lists them as Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, Pliny the Elder, Strabo and Pomponius Mela, the Roman geographer, and says these writers span roughly 500 BC up to the first century AD. the article's cited researcher, Sean Rigby's article puts the count at six ancient authors who mention the Labyrinth: Herodotus, Strabo, the 3rd century BC priest Manetho, the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus of the 1st century BC, the Roman writer Pliny the Elder of about AD 23 to 79, and the Roman geographer Pomponius Mela, writing around AD 43. The Historic Mysteries article gives almost the same roster and makes the point that Herodotus was not the first historian to describe ancient Egypt's labyrinth. It names Manetho Aegyptiaca in the 3rd century BC, Diodorus Siculus in the 1st century BC, Strabo from 64 BC to 19 AD, Pliny from 23 to 79 AD, and Pomponius Mela around 43 AD, and says at least two of them claimed to have visited the labyrinth themselves. Rigby's framing is that the Egyptian 'Labyrinth' is a largely vanished monument that greatly impressed Classical writers.

The sources do not agree on when Herodotus was there. Rigby dates him c.484 to 425 BC. The compilation on the Archaeological Rescue Foundation page, excerpted from Louis De Cordier's Mataha Expedition report, dates him ca. 484 to 430 BC. The Why Files episode puts him at Hawara around 450 BC. Johanna, on her own channel, says he went there at "like 150 AD I think or BC, one of them," and she flags her own uncertainty as she says it. Her date does not match any of the others. What all of them agree on is the claim itself. Writing in his Histories in the fifth century BC, Herodotus said the labyrinth surpassed the pyramids in grandeur. The quote the Rogan guest reads out runs: "For this I saw myself and I found it greater than words can say. For if one should put together and reckon up all the buildings and all of the great works produced by the Hellenes, the Greeks, they would prove to be inferior in labor and expense to this labyrinth." The fuller version in the De Cordier compilation adds that the temple at Ephesos and the temple at Samos are works worthy of note, that the pyramids too were greater than words can say, and that the labyrinth surpasses even the pyramids. Rigby quotes the same passage in a different translation: "I have seen it myself, and indeed words cannot describe it. Though the pyramids beggar description and each one of them is a match for many great monuments built by Greeks, this maze surpasses even the pyramids." The Historic Mysteries version has Herodotus saying in the second book of his Histories that this was a work he had never seen before, a work that defied description, and that even the Greeks' vast monuments and the pyramids paled by comparison.

On the layout, Herodotus reported twelve roofed courts with doors facing each other, six facing north and six facing south, all inside one outer wall, and double sets of chambers totalling three thousand, fifteen hundred above ground and fifteen hundred underground. The Archaeological Rescue Foundation compilation gives the same numbers and describes the twelve courts as having gates facing one another. Herodotus wrote that the roof over the whole thing was made of stone, like the walls, which is the line De Cordier picks out from Histories Book II, 148. He also wrote that at the corner where the labyrinth ends there stood a pyramid of forty fathoms, with large figures carved on it, and a way made underground to it. The video about the tunnels under Giza renders that same passage as a pyramid 240 feet in height with carved figures of animals on it and an underground passage by which it can be entered, and adds that Herodotus was told these underground chambers connect the pyramid with the pyramids at Memphis. That video then identifies the Memphis he meant as the Giza Plateau today. That identification is the video's own gloss, not something in the quoted passage.

Herodotus was clear about what he did and did not see. The upper set of chambers he walked through himself. The chambers underground he heard about only, because the Egyptians who had charge of them were not willing on any account to show them, saying that here were the sepulchres of the kings who had first built the labyrinth and of the sacred crocodiles. The Why Files episode covers this and adds detail the Herodotus quotation does not carry: it says the priests told him the lower levels held the burial vaults of sacred crocodiles, mummified, wrapped in linen with bronze teeth and eyes made of jewels. The bronze teeth and jewelled eyes are the episode's dressing. The underlying quotation, which the episode itself reads out a moment later, says only sepulchres of the kings and of the sacred crocodiles. The Historic Mysteries piece takes a different line again and says Herodotus claimed to have counted three thousand rooms, with walls covered in hieroglyphs and paintings, making up a funerary complex hidden beneath a pyramid. Counting all three thousand sits awkwardly with Herodotus's own statement that half of them were described to him rather than shown.

On location, Herodotus placed the Labyrinth a little way beyond Lake Moeris and near the place called the City of Crocodiles, which Rigby identifies as Arsinoë, capital of the Fayum, and he wrote that near the corner where the Labyrinth ends stands a pyramid. The Rogan guest gives the same two markers, Lake Moeris and a city called Crocodilopolis, also known as ancient Arsinoe. Strabo placed it differently. He wrote that the Labyrinth had adjoining to it the tomb of the king who constructed it, and that he came across it after proceeding beyond the first entrance of the canal joining the Nile to Lake Moeris about 30 or 40 stadia, where there is a table-shaped plain with a village and a large palace.

Strabo, dated c.64 BC to AD 24 by Rigby and ca. 64 BC to 19 CE in the De Cordier compilation, called the Labyrinth "a work equal to the Pyramids," a building containing peristyle courts equal in number to the nomes of Egypt, with hidden chambers so twisting that no one could enter or leave without a guide. De Cordier cites him as Geography, Book 17, I, 3 and 37, the passage in which Strabo wrote that the roofs of each chamber were made of single stones. The Why Files episode, which puts him about four centuries after Herodotus, says he found the labyrinth still there and still in use. His description is of a large palace composed of as many sub-palaces, the aulae, as there were nomes, arranged contiguously in one line, with the entrances into the courts opposite a long wall, and with long winding covered ways in front of the entrances so that no stranger could find his way in or out without a guide. The roofs of each chamber were made of single stones, and the covered ways were roofed the same way with single slabs of extraordinary size, with no timber or any other material included. Looking down into the aulae from the roof, they lie in a row each supported by twenty-seven pillars, each consisting of a single stone, and the walls are of stones no smaller. De Cordier's excerpt of Strabo also records that the total number of nomes was equal to the number of courts in the Labyrinth, and that these are fewer than 30. The Why Files reduces the roof detail to a roof made of a single stone with no wood or other material involved, then dramatizes it as millions of tons of rock floating over their heads. The stone-slab roofing is in Strabo. The floating rock is the episode talking.

Diodorus Siculus, writing in the 1st century BC, said in his History, Book I, 61 and 66, that the building had a roof made of a single stone. He wrote that when the king died and the government was recovered by Egyptians, they appointed a native king Mendes, whom some call Mares, and that this king built what is called the Labyrinth as a tomb. He added that it is said by some that Daedalus crossed over to Egypt and, in wonder at the skill shown in the building, built for Minos, King of Crete, a labyrinth like the Egyptian one, in which the Minotaur was kept, and that unlike the Cretan Labyrinth, which has completely disappeared, the Egyptian Labyrinth remained absolutely perfect in its entire construction down to his own time. Wikipedia's Hawara page states flatly that there is no historicity to the assertion of Diodorus Siculus that this was the model for the labyrinth of Crete that the Greeks imagined housed the Minotaur. The Why Files episode says Diodorus Siculus and Pliny the Elder wrote about the labyrinth over a hundred years after Strabo. That ordering does not fit the 1st century BC date every other source here gives Diodorus, and the sources are left disagreeing about it.

Pliny the Elder said the Cretan labyrinth of Daedalus was only a hundredth-part copy of the Egyptian one. Rigby quotes him from Naturalis Historia 36.13: "that Daedalus used this as the model for the Labyrinth which he built in Crete is beyond doubt, but it is equally clear that he imitated only the hundredth part of it which contains twisting paths and passages, all impossible to negotiate." The Why Files gives the same claim in its own wording, that the famous Greek labyrinth was just a cheap copy. Manetho, by contrast, referred to the Labyrinth merely as a 'tomb'. Alan Lloyd, the Egyptologist citing Herodotus, has suggested that only Herodotus and Strabo actually visited the site, and that the other ancient accounts were second-hand, based on hearsay.

The ancient accounts do not reconcile. Rigby's article says plainly that the accounts of Herodotus and Strabo, the two authors usually treated as the more reliable sources, differ significantly on the fundamental number of courts or chambers. Flinders Petrie suggested the total number of nomes in Egypt was 42, with 22 in the Fayum alone, and that figure does not match either man's numbers closely. Some of the uncertainty comes from translation. Where the text is rendered 'roofed courts', Herodotus used a term transliterated as aulae katastegoi, and Alan Lloyd regards that as a contradiction in terms, since aula normally meant an open courtyard before a house while katastegoi means roofed-over. One explanation offered is that the roofed part was a peripheral colonnade surrounding an otherwise open space, and that Herodotus was struggling to describe unfamiliar Egyptian architecture in terms his Greek readers could follow. Attempts to reconcile the two men have also suggested that Herodotus only got to see the outer part of the complex while Strabo was allowed further in, perhaps because the outer parts had been destroyed in the meantime. Rigby's conclusion is that the over-exaggerated ancient descriptions likely arose from Graeco-Roman unfamiliarity with Egyptian architecture and from sensationalized attempts to describe it in terms a Graeco-Roman readership would find impressive, and that until much more systematic and wide-ranging modern excavation is carried out, a reliably authentic reconstruction of the Labyrinth is not possible.

Historic Mysteries takes the opposite posture. It calls Herodotus one of our most useful sources on the ancient world, says his writings are usually reliable, and notes he is often the only source we have for certain ancient events and places. It records that he claimed to have personally visited a labyrinth in Egypt during his travels. It also says many historians had considered his description of the labyrinth to be a rare instance of unreliability from him, and that recent discoveries have thrown doubt on that interpretation. The same article notes that Amenemhat III built the pyramid in the 19th century BC, so that when Herodotus visited the site it was already more than a thousand years old.

Wikipedia's Hawara entry gives the sober version of the same story. The huge mortuary temple that originally stood adjacent to the pyramid is believed to have formed the basis of the complex of buildings with galleries and courtyards called the "Labyrinth" by Herodotus, and this building was also mentioned by Strabo and Diodorus Siculus. The Mataha Expedition page describes Hawara as the site believed to house the legendary Egyptian Labyrinth, a colossal structure described by Herodotus, Strabo and Pliny as surpassing even the pyramids in grandeur. The article recounting that expedition opens by noting that more than 2,000 years ago the ancient Greek historians Herodotus and Strabo recorded their visits to the legendary labyrinth of Egypt.

The Why Files episode compresses all of this into a single sweep. For a thousand years, historians traveled to Egypt to see the famous labyrinth of Hawara, and they said it was so massive it made the pyramids look small. The episode puts its size at about 3 million square feet, 70 acres of rooms and corridors stacked on multiple levels. Historians wrote about it for 600 years, across different eras, different languages and different cultures, and they all described the same thing. Herodotus, the episode says, reported that the construction was beyond human ability and that it surpassed even the pyramids and all the buildings of the Greeks combined. The upper floor alone was massive, and around the maze of rooms were 12 enormous chambers called courts, each representing one of Egypt's regional governments. There were 3,000 chambers in total, above and below ground, and the underground ones were not shown to him. The Egyptian priests allowed visitors on the upper floors but kept the chambers below ground off limits, saying those rooms belonged to the kings who built the labyrinth. And the episode makes a point of the one detail every historian agrees on: nobody was allowed to enter the lower chambers, and for 2,000 years nobody did.

Johanna's video gives the version she found in the historical record. Around the Hawara pyramid, she says, is a huge underground labyrinth with two floors and up to 3,000 chambers, and it was the place where they stored the antiquities, the secrets and all of the pre-Egyptian history. She reads Herodotus at length, then reads a second passage she also attributes to him: "when one had entered the sacred enclosure one found a temple surrounded by columns 40 to each side, and this building had a roof made of a single stone carved with panels and richly adorned with excellent paintings. It contained memorials of the homeland of each of the kings as well as the temples and the sacrifices carried out in it, all skillfully worked in paintings of the greatest beauty." That same passage appears word for word in the De Cordier compilation, where it is attributed to Diodorus Siculus, History Book I, 61 and 66, not to Herodotus. The two sources disagree on whose words those are. What catches Johanna is the phrase "memorials of the homeland." She wonders aloud whether 'homeland' means Atlantis, and grounds the guess in Egyptian oral tradition recorded at the Temple of Edfu, which she says holds that the Egyptians were survivors of a deluge from an island that disappeared in a day and a night, after which they traveled to Egypt, recolonized and restarted Egyptian civilization. She presents that as her own speculation, not as something the ancient text says.

Johanna also found a labyrinth reference she says is otherwise hard to come by. It is in the Apocryphal Acts of Thomas the Apostle, a non-canonical ancient text originally written in Aramaic and also translated into Greek, which she says is included in the Eastern Orthodox and African Orthodox Church traditions. The text contains a hymn about a man who travels to Egypt to find a pearl. One passage speaks of a letter sealed by the king against the evil children of Babylon and "the Savage Demons of the Sarbug Labyrinth." Another translation renders the same line as the wicked Babylonians and "the tyrannical Demons of the labyrinth." Johanna notes that Sarbug is an old name for a city in Iran, which raises the possibility that multiple labyrinths existed in different ancient locations rather than one. She also suggests that legends of demons guarding a labyrinth would have worked as a security deterrent, keeping people away from valuable or secret contents, on the reasoning that most people would not go down there if they believed demons were waiting.

In her later conversation with Trevor Grassi, Johanna sets out the same site in a short summary. The labyrinth is described as thousands of underground chambers and complex runs of corridors, potentially including tombs of the earliest pharaohs, and she says historical records claim the legend of the labyrinth goes back into antiquity, potentially even before the dynastic Egyptians themselves. In the same conversation the labyrinth is described as big enough to stick half the temples of Egypt inside of it.

The Archaeological Rescue Foundation page, written by Trevor Grassi with excerpts by Louis De Cordier, sums up the ancient testimony as an endless progression of halls, galleries, palaces, tombs and libraries, impossible to navigate without a guide, with temples to all the Gods of Egypt housed within thousands of chambers on multiple levels descending into the earth. It also restates Herodotus's numbers for the Hawara Labyrinth as 3,000 chambers, 1,500 above ground and 1,500 below, arranged in 12 courts with gates facing one another, and repeats that he called it superior to the works of the Greeks including the temples at Ephesos and Samos.

The AncientHistoryX article, reporting the start of official excavation, calls the target the legendary Labyrinth of Amenemhat III, the colossal temple complex Herodotus called greater than the pyramids themselves. It describes the goal as locating and documenting any surviving remains of the enormous "Palace of the Labyrinth" that ancient writers described as having thousands of rooms, courts and passages, half above ground and half below. It says Petrie's 1888 survey mapped a foundation of roughly 277,000 square feet, big enough to match Herodotus's awe-struck account, and argues that confirming even part of the layout would prove Herodotus was not exaggerating after all. That 277,000 square foot figure is much smaller than the 3 million square feet, or 70 acres, the Why Files gives for the same building. The two numbers are left standing against each other in the sources.

files.title: Early excavations and early surveys at Hawara
files.body:
The region is called the Faiyum. In the Joe Rogan Experience conversation it is described as a leaf-shaped depression west of the Nile Valley, green on the map where everything around it is desert, a place that used to flood with the Nile and is now used for agriculture. Hawara sits at the neck of that depression where it connects back to the Nile Valley, and the pyramid of Amenemhat III stands on the site.

The sources do not agree on how far Hawara is from Cairo, and it is worth putting the numbers side by side rather than picking one. The Why Files episode says Hawara sits at the edge of the Faiyum Oasis about 50 miles south of Cairo, near a crumbling black pyramid, and that today it looks like a pile of rubble. Johanna's video, whose main topic is the Hawara site, puts it about 100 miles south of Cairo. The Historic Mysteries article, titled "Herodotus and the Lost Labyrinth of Egypt: Found at Last?", says the complex is located less than 100 kilometers from Cairo. The Archaeological Rescue Foundation's plan document measures it differently again, calling Hawara an archaeological site at the entrance to the Fayoum Oasis, roughly 90 kilometers south of the Giza Plateau. There is also a wrinkle in the Why Files line about the black pyramid. The Wikipedia entry places the Black Pyramid at Dahshur, says the Hawara pyramid is believed to post-date it, and in describing Petrie's work explicitly separates the pyramid of Amenemhat III at Hawara from the Black Pyramid.

The Wikipedia entry gives the flat description. Hawara is an archaeological site of Ancient Egypt located south of Crocodilopolis, also called Arsinoë and known today as Medinet al-Faiyum, at the entrance to the depression of the Fayyum oasis. It is the site of a pyramid built by King Amenemhat III of the 12th dynasty, between the 19th and 18th centuries BC. Amenemhat III was the last powerful ruler of the 12th Dynasty. The pyramid at Hawara is believed to post-date the Black Pyramid he built at Dahshur, and is believed to have been his final resting place. The intact pyramid tomb of Neferuptah, his daughter, was found at Hawara about 2 kilometers south of the king's pyramid. The two-part feature on the Mataha expedition sets the geography out the same way and adds detail on the neighbouring city. The City of Crocodiles, also called Crocodilopolis, was an ancient city in the Heptanomis on the western bank of the Nile, between the river and Lake Moeris, southwest of Memphis, and Hawara sits just south of it at the entrance to the depression of the Faiyum Oasis. Sean Rigby's magazine article notes that Hawara holds the eroded mud-brick core of the pyramid of the Twelfth Dynasty pharaoh Amenemhat III, dated there to about 1855 to 1808 BC, and that this is likely the tomb Strabo mentioned. The Historic Mysteries article says the Pyramid of Hawara was constructed by Amenemhat III, the last great ruler of Egypt's 12th dynasty at the height of the unified Middle Kingdom period.

On how the pyramid was built and what became of it, the Wikipedia entry says that in common with Middle Kingdom pyramids built after Amenemhat II, it was constructed of mudbrick around a core of limestone passages and burial chambers, and faced with limestone. Most of that limestone facing was later pillaged for use in other buildings, a fate common to almost all of Egypt's pyramids. Today the pyramid is little more than an eroded, vaguely pyramidal mountain of mud brick, and of the once magnificent mortuary temple precinct there is little left beyond the foundation bed of compacted sand and chips and shards of limestone. Johanna's video describes the same thing from the ground. She points out that Hawara is an oasis within the Sahara, unlike most of the desert around it, that the pyramid was built from mud brick rather than the harder stone of the Giza Pyramids, and that little remains visible above ground. What she stresses is that the interior and the underground portions are megalithic and remain intact. You can no longer go inside, she says, because a rising water table has flooded it, the Nile having once flowed right up near the pyramid.

The Wikipedia entry also carries the demolition history. The demolition of the Labyrinth may date in part to the reign of Ptolemy II, under whom the Pharaonic city of Shedyt, Greek Crocodilopolis, modern Medinet el-Fayum, was renamed to honour his sister-wife Arsinoë. A massive Ptolemaic building program at Arsinoë has been suggested as the ultimate destination of Middle Kingdom limestone columns and blocks removed from Hawara and now lost. The entry adds that Pharaoh Sobekneferu of the 12th Dynasty also built at the Hawara complex, and that her name meant "most beautiful of Sobek", the sacred crocodile. The Historic Mysteries article puts it more loosely, saying little remains of the original labyrinth structure today, that much of it was demolished by later Egyptian dynasties who pillaged it for dressed stone and other building materials, and that what remains now is little more than a ghostly outline on the landscape. That article also offers a reading of what the building was for. The labyrinth appears to have originally been a huge mortuary temple, and the Egyptians would have used its many rooms for funerary rites and cult worship of the dead pharaoh associated with the nearby royal tomb. The Why Files episode compresses all of this into one line, that the labyrinth was eventually looted and quarried for stone, which led archaeologists to claim nothing remained but rubble and sand.

Karl Lepsius comes first in the survey history, and the sources describe his conclusion in two different ways. The Joe Rogan conversation says Lepsius surveyed the site in the 1700s, found the ruins of a Roman town built on the surface, and concluded there was nothing significant there. Sean Rigby's article says the Prussian Egyptologist Karl Richard Lepsius gave the most thorough nineteenth-century account, that he observed a great platform on which the pyramid and the buildings south of it had once stood, and that he found Roman mud-brick remains which he mistakenly identified as the Labyrinth. So one source has him dismissing the site and the other has him claiming to have found the very thing. The dates do not line up either. The Rogan conversation puts him in the 1700s, while the Wikipedia entry says the labyrinth was first located in modern times by Karl Lepsius in 1843.

Flinders Petrie is the centre of this part of the story. The Joe Rogan conversation says he excavated at Hawara in the late 1800s and early 1900s and dug down seven or eight meters, where he found a massive stone slab of beton or plaster roughly a thousand feet long. He traced its edges and concluded he was standing on the foundation of the labyrinth, and that the building above it had been quarried away and destroyed. That conversation is explicit about the consequence. Since Petrie's conclusion, orthodox Egyptology and sources like Wikipedia have stated that the labyrinth was destroyed or quarried away and no longer exists.

The Why Files episode tells Petrie's dig as a set piece, with a comic sidekick interrupting the narration and lines written for dramatic effect, so the performance is the episode's own. The underlying facts it is dramatising sit in Petrie's own account and in the Wikipedia entry. Petrie discovered that the pyramid was made of mud brick held together by loose sand, which made it unstable, and that it was rigged with traps, including sliding trap doors, false passages, and stones set to drop on intruders. After tunnelling south he found a door with steps leading underground, though the steps were submerged in salty, filthy water because centuries of canal irrigation had raised the water table. He reached a central chamber carved from a single block of yellow quartzite, roofed with three quartzite slabs each weighing 45 tons, and found it empty, because tomb robbers had already looted it. Then, studying the field of rubble beside the pyramid, he found the remains of a building covering 70 acres, and the location matched ancient maps and the dimensions matched ancient descriptions, so he concluded he was standing on the foundation of the lost labyrinth of Hawara. The episode says he believed the labyrinth was destroyed and went back to England disappointed, not realising that what he had found was only the roof of a structure that extended much further underground. That last step, the roof reading, is the episode's claim rather than Petrie's.

The Wikipedia entry lays out the trap system in detail, and its account of how Petrie found it differs from the Why Files version. From the pyramid entrance a sloping passageway with steps runs down to a small room and then a further short horizontal passage. Hidden in the roof of that horizontal passage was a concealed sliding trapdoor weighing 20 tons. If a robber found and opened it, he would meet either an empty passage closed by wooden doors or a parallel passage carefully filled with mud and stone blocking, which was designed to make him waste time clearing it. A second 20-ton trapdoor sat in the roof of the empty passage and gave onto a second empty passage at a right angle to the first. A third 20-ton trapdoor gave onto a passage at a right angle to its predecessor, so the passages circled the interior of the pyramid. The final passage ended in a large area of mud and stone blocking that presumably concealed the burial chamber, but this was a blind, filling a wide but shallow alcove. Two blind shafts in the floor, carefully filled with cut stone blocks, wasted the robbers' time further. The real entrance to the burial chamber lay between the blind shafts and opposite the alcove. Despite all of it, Petrie found that none of the trapdoors had been slid into place and that the wooden doors were open. That is a plain difference from the Why Files line about Petrie disarming the traps one by one.

The burial chamber itself was made from a single quartzite monolith lowered into a larger chamber lined with limestone. Petrie estimated the monolithic slab at 110 tons. A course of brick was placed on the chamber to raise the ceiling, and then the chamber was covered with 3 quartzite slabs estimated at 45 tons each. Above the burial chamber were 2 relieving chambers, topped with 50-ton limestone slabs forming a pointed roof, and over that an enormous arch of brick 3 feet thick was built to support the core of the pyramid. When it was found there were two sarcophagi in the quartzite monolith burial chamber, with room for at least two more. When Petrie excavated the chamber he found a bead of lapis lazuli for inlaying, burned bone fragments, burned wood, and charcoal, which suggests tomb robbers had burned the wooden coffins and the mummy of the pharaoh.

Johanna's video describes the same interior in different mineral terms. She says that in the 1800s Petrie excavated the Hawara pyramid when the water table was lower, and that he found a large yellow-stone calcite box, alabaster, precision-made, similar to boxes found in the Saqqara tunnel system. She adds that huge yellow calcite slabs line the interior of the pyramid, a feature she says she has not seen in other Egyptian pyramids, and that calcite or alabaster has conductive properties. She does not take the science further than the assertion. Note that where she says calcite and alabaster, the Why Files episode and the Wikipedia entry both call the chamber stone quartzite. Johanna also covers the slab. In the 1800s, she says, Petrie found a huge stone slab he believed was the foundation of the labyrinth structure, and concluded it had been destroyed over time.

North of the pyramid Petrie found a vast necropolis containing 146 portraits on coffins dating to the Roman period, the "Fayum" mummy portraits, considered among the very few surviving examples of painted portraits from classical antiquity. Among his discoveries was a great papyrus scroll containing parts of books 1 and 2 of the Iliad, known as the "Hawara Homer", now held at the Bodleian Library in Oxford. The Wikipedia entry says Petrie's first excavation at Hawara can be retraced in four overlapping phases. Phase 1 was the excavation of the Pyramid of Amenemhat III itself, which is distinct from the Black Pyramid. Phase 2 was a survey of the "Site of the Labyrinth", cut short after only limited discoveries, after which the excavation's resources were redirected to the pyramid and the surrounding tombs. Phase 3 began after a painted portrait was discovered in the "Scattered Tombs" north of the pyramid, and Petrie was quick to see the worth of it. "If we can get one or two a week," he wrote in his journal, "we shall be well repaid." He was also interested in potential eugenic interpretations of the artefacts, and wrote a letter to his fellow eugenicist Francis Galton discussing his findings. After increasing pressure from competition posed by other antiquities dealers, Petrie finished excavating both the pyramid and the northern cemetery. Phase 4 entailed the excavation of the "very promising" "Crocodile Tomb-Chapels" north-east of the pyramid.

The measurements of the slab differ between sources, though two of them agree. The two-part Mataha feature says Petrie discovered an enormous artificial stone plateau measuring 304m by 244m, that is 304 meters by 244 meters,, that he interpreted it as the foundation of the labyrinth, and that he concluded the labyrinth itself must have been destroyed in antiquity, leaving only the stone base. Sean Rigby's article gives the same figures in imperial, writing that Petrie estimated the main rectangular structure at about 1,000 by 800 feet, 304 by 244 metres, a size that would make it bigger than the temple of Karnak. Against that, the Rogan conversation gives only a rough thousand feet long, and the Why Files episode gives 70 acres.

Rigby's article carries the fullest account of what Petrie actually mapped on the labyrinth site. Petrie found the rectangle divided roughly in half from east to west by a wall running along its middle, and he unearthed the foundations of a great retaining wall at the southern end. Along the western boundary he found the ruined traces of two stone walls separated by a space. In the southern area, close to the extended middle axis of the pyramid, he discovered a large quartzite sandstone door jamb, which suggested a great entrance to the Labyrinth building. Column fragments suggested the roof had been barrel-vaulted, and red granite columns were found only north of the central dividing wall. The presence of stone building fragments suggested the site was a temple rather than a palace or an administrative centre, since those would typically have been built in mud brick. The site was identified as built by Amenemhat III because of fragments of red granite architraves bearing his cartouche and the name of his daughter Sobekneferu, found within the pyramid enclosure. South of the pyramid, just east of the central axis, two red granite shrines were found, with remnants of another to the west, and each of them contained two sculpted figures of Amenemhat III. Further statue fragments east and south-east of the shrines included white limestone statues of the goddess Hathor, the god Sobek, a goddess wearing a headdress of four palms or feathers, and Amenemhat III with two goddesses holding fish. North-east of the pyramid a great cemetery area was found containing shaft-tombs and mastabas, which Petrie called "the area of crocodile burials", and which may correspond to the pteron, or "wing", mentioned by Pliny.

Petrie also tried to reconstruct the building. He developed a reconstruction of the Labyrinth combining his own observations, those of Lepsius, and the ancient textual descriptions. He accepted that the chamber layout he reconstructed bore no resemblance to the typical ground-plan of Egyptian temples, and he proposed that this was exactly what caused the confusion of ancient visitors and, from there, the association with the Cretan Labyrinth.

Eric Parrington Uphill, who lived from 1929 to 2018, proposed an alternative reconstruction. He worked by comparison, setting Hawara against the other known Twelfth Dynasty pyramid complexes of Amenemhat I, Senusret I, Amenemhat II, Senusret II and Senusret III, and against the second pyramid complex Amenemhat III built for himself at Dahshur. Uphill proposed that the Labyrinth was much smaller than the earlier descriptions suggested, consisting of a dock and quay, a valley temple, a causeway, and a mortuary temple with a colonnaded court and a sanctuary containing the royal shrines. He proposed that the causeway was lined on both sides by arrays of three subsidiary pyramids for queens, with walled enclosures containing funerary shrines, passageways and storage chambers, and that these two sets of six structures could correspond to Herodotus's 12 covered courts. He also suggested that Herodotus's reported 1,500 chambers likely included chambers from the mastabas and tombs north-east of the pyramid rather than the mortuary temple complex alone, and that Herodotus may have over-schematised his account.

Two of the popular sources read the site the other way, as confirmation. The Historic Mysteries article says the complex discovered at Hawara matches Herodotus's description both in location and construction, and that it comprises around 3,000 rooms packed with hieroglyphs and murals, just as Herodotus described. The AncientHistoryX write-up, looking back over the geophysical and satellite work that preceded the 2026 dig, describes those prior studies as careful, qualified science that stuck to what the technology could actually detect, which was shallow subsurface features in dry desert soil. That same write-up says the site today looks quiet, showing only the weathered mud-brick core of the pyramid rising from the sand.

files.title: The Mataha Expedition and the modern subsurface scans
files.body:
The podcast guest starts with a video he had just put out on his own YouTube channel, the one about an ancient structure said to be greater than the pyramids. He had covered the labyrinth before in a much longer video, and he had been wanting to revisit it for a long time. What brought him back was new data. The main piece was the Merlin Burrow scans, which lined up with other scans and reported a metallic object underground. He stresses that this is not crazy emerging science. Merlin Burrow, he says, is a legitimate company using technology that came out of UK defense and military work and is more or less proven. The man who examined the scan data was a man named Tim Acres, who has since passed away. The guest calls him credible and says Acres drew no conclusion about what the object might be. What Acres would say is that it is definitely metal. Not wood. Not stone. The exact type of metal could not be classified. The object sits in a central atrium. The guest describes the labyrinth as having multiple levels that all connect to one large central chamber, the way a shopping mall atrium does. That atrium is open, at least 40 meters long and very tall, and the thing sitting in the middle of it is a single piece about 40 meters long.

On the expedition itself, the same interview says the Mataha Expedition was funded and driven by Louis De Cordier, a Belgian artist and entrepreneur. He ran it in conjunction with the Supreme Council of Antiquities, headed at the time by Zahi Hawass, and with the National Research Institute for subsurface studies, NRIAG. The team used a spread of techniques: ground-penetrating radar, geomagnetism, very low frequency sounding, seismic tomography and electrical resistivity tomography. Near the surface they found what matches Lepsius's description of a Roman, Greek and Persian era town built with mud bricks. Below that comes the water table, which sits about 5 meters down. Under the water, at roughly 6 to 7 meters, is the huge slab Petrie found and believed was the foundation. Petrie did not dig deeper. Below the slab, the expedition's VLF sounding at 8 meters depth showed a labyrinthine structure of granite with walls meters thick. The scanned section measures about 150 meters across, and they scanned two separate areas at the site. The guest says the overall structure is much larger than the sections they covered, potentially at least 1,000 feet in scale, three to five times larger. One scanned area was in front of the pyramid. The other was on the other side of the canal that runs through the site today, and they found structure on both sides. He calls the labyrinth potentially the biggest archaeological discovery of the millennium, and says it would be like finding another Giza plateau underground.

The Why Files episode covers the same ground as entertainment. Its cold open says archaeologists call the labyrinth a myth, and that new technology proves it still exists underground. That second half is the narration's claim, not something it sources. The episode's account of the 2008 work is that De Cordier's radar could see through 50 feet of sand and sediment, and that it found a massive grid of granite walls 40 feet down covering about 750,000 square feet, roughly the size of 10 football fields. Then it moves to Acres, whose name it renders as Akers, and stages the reveal as a scene at a private meeting in the Crown Hotel in England on July 21st, 2015. The scan behind the dramatization is the Merlin Burrows work described elsewhere. What the episode says that scan showed is four levels beneath the labyrinth's roof, separated by up to 100 feet of solid rock and connected by a central vertical shaft extending 150 feet underground. An omega-shaped moat surrounds the structure, matching the Egyptian Shen ring, the symbol of eternity. The bottom level of the complex stretches 300 feet long and 120 feet wide, and all the levels converge on a central hall. At the center of that hall, Akers's team detected a freestanding object about 130 feet long with a metallic radar signature, unlike stone, wood or mud brick. Akers described it as shaped like an upright disc or ring, roughly the size of the Statue of Liberty. His team speculated that it could be a portal or a power generator rather than a coffin. Note that the Why Files gives its figures in feet where the other sources give meters.

Johanna's video makes the basic point first. The Labyrinth of Egypt, long thought to be myth, is a real site located at or near Hawara, and it was rediscovered 13 years before she made the video. She says the project was called the Mataha Expedition, that it had a website, and that a company was preparing to render the ground-penetrating radar data into visual imagery. About two years after the block came down, the team decided to release some of their findings anyway. She found a copy of the report. What it shows, she says, is a grid structure of gigantic size at a depth of 8 to 12 meters below the surface, made of a very high resistivity material resembling granite. The grid is also out of angle by 20 to 25 degrees from the orientation of the Hawara pyramid, which she takes as a sign the labyrinth may predate the pyramid. One difference is worth keeping. Johanna calls De Cordier a French artist, while the podcast interview and the written sources call him Belgian.

Johanna's later video is a call with Trevor Grassi, the man who first told her about the structures found under a pyramid. He says that over the last 20 years multiple scanning projects using different technologies have produced correlating data showing that structures exist underground at Hawara. The scans also show that the first few sub-levels of the labyrinth are water filled, while the chambers below that appear to be water free. That reading came from the researcher Carmen Boulter, who analyzed scans in which the blue areas were flooded and the red areas were not. Grassi adds that when diggers went down at the corner of the pyramid they found the original stone corner deep underground, which reveals the pyramid to be much bigger than previously thought. The visible mud-brick structure is then either a decomposed outer layer or a protective covering over a full stone megalithic core pyramid underneath, and he favors the second reading. He points to Dr. Shock and his wife Katie, who have proposed that mud brick coverings at many Egyptian sites were intentional protective burials over older stone structures. There is also a shaft, and it leads down to labyrinth chambers below the flooded levels that are reportedly not flooded. On what comes next, Filippo, through his scanning company, had already promised to scan Hawara right after he finished Giza. Two other companies, Geoscan and Merlin Burroughs, claim they can scan kilometers deep and have done that kind of work for oil and mineral extraction companies, but they require permission signatures from the landowners before they could scan Giza. Grassi is also working on a project called the digital dig, which aims to build a distributed computing network so volunteers online can donate processing power and help process the ground-scan signals faster. As things stand, it has taken Filippo two years to process about 200 images of Giza using two computers running continuously. Near the surface at Hawara, Grassi says, there are intact wooden ships similar to Khufu's solar boat, along with Roman-era artifacts. Once they can get in, the team plans to create a complete photogrammetric and laser-scanned 360-degree virtual model of everything discovered underground at Hawara, without touching any artifacts.

The Mataha Foundation's own page states the question the expedition set out to answer. It aimed to resolve whether the labyrinth was truly destroyed or still lies hidden beneath the sands. It used Ground Penetrating Radar, or GPR. It was led by NRIAG, the National Research Institute of Astronomy and Geophysics in Egypt, and by Ghent University. The page says the expedition uncovered scientific evidence of an enormous underground structure at Hawara, and that the findings challenged the long-held belief that the labyrinth had been completely dismantled in antiquity. A vast complex of interconnected walls and chambers was detected beneath the surface at the site, and the page says the detected structure aligns with ancient descriptions of the labyrinth. It points readers to the full official results and whitepapers, in a document it links as labyrinthofegypt_com__printversion.pdf.

The Ancient Origins write-up gives the reasoning behind the survey. Louis de Cordier, researcher and coordinator of the Mataha expedition, questioned Petrie's conclusion that the stone slab was the foundation. He proposed that the large slab might actually be the roof of the labyrinth, with the entire complex hidden beneath it. Breaking through the slab risked great damage to the site, so the expedition aimed to explore the area below it using ground-penetrating radar instead, to avoid damaging the site. The testing was conducted after receiving permission from the Supreme Council of Antiquities of Egypt, then headed by Dr Zahi Hawass. The radar surveys revealed a strong suggestion of a vast number of chambers and walls several metres thick. Below the stone slab, at a depth of 8 to 12 metres, the surveys found a grid structure of gigantic size made of a very high resistivity material such as granite. The article reads those geophysics research findings as consistent with descriptions of the lost labyrinth of Egypt. It also gives the publication trail. The findings were published in the fall 2008 scientific journal of the NRIAG. Louis de Cordier, the expedition lead, waited two years for the Supreme Council to make the findings public. He then launched his own website, Labyrinth of Egypt, to publicly post the research results. In the comments under that article, one commenter states their belief that Petrie misidentified the stone slab as the floor of the labyrinth when it was actually the roof, and another claims that LiDAR and similar surveys have concluded there are stone structures underneath the sand at the site.

The AncientHistoryX post covers the dig now under way. It says the excavations follow decades of geophysical surveys, satellite scans and advocacy from researchers including the Mataha Foundation and Archaeological Rescue teams. The excavation target is the legendary Labyrinth of Amenemhat III, a colossal temple complex. Egyptian antiquities authorities have mobilized a team to dig where the massive structure once stood, next to the pyramid of the 12th Dynasty pharaoh Amenemhat III, and the post describes that pyramid as crumbling. Ashraf Sobhi, Director General of Fayoum Antiquities, is overseeing the mission, which includes a team of inspectors and archaeologists from the Supreme Council of Antiquities. The post also lists the earlier SAR studies it builds on: Carlotto's 2023 work, Merlin Burrows' 2015 imagery, and the 2008 Mataha VLF-EM survey. Those earlier studies suggested buried rectangular chambers and thick walls south of the pyramid.

The Archaeological Rescue Foundation's page is the fullest catalogue of the scans. Its updates report that the Khafre Research Project held a press conference to disclose the final report on their SAR scans of the Giza Plateau, and that Filippo Biondi agreed to scan the Hawara Labyrinth next. They also hold hours of footage of Timothy Akers, the ARF-linked researcher, recorded before he passed by Michael Donnelan, explaining his own scans of Hawara in every detail. Taking the scans in order, William Brown's scans showed that the pyramid structure extended deep under the sand, larger than previously known, because he found its real underground corner. Brown, a civil engineer, also conducted the first analysis of the groundwater at Hawara by drilling bore holes at strategic points. For the Mataha Expedition, Dr. Abbas Mohamed Abbas, the GPR survey collaborator, led the scans with the National Research Institute of Astronomy and Geophysics of Egypt, in partnership with Ghent University of Belgium, and Louis De Cordier wrote a report covering the history of the labyrinth from Herodotus to Sir William Flinders Petrie, plus the results of the expedition's scans. The first satellite-based scan was by GeoScan Systems, organized by Dr. Carmen Boulter, with help from Louis De Cordier, Andrew Barker, Klaus Dona and Michael Donnelan. Boulter's team produced a virtual model from the satellite data showing two separated levels of the labyrinth, a flooded blue level above and a non-flooded red level below, which is the same reading Grassi described to Johanna. Mark Carlotto compiled two papers about satellite-based SAR sensing that include information about Carmen Boulter's work. A fourth scan was led by Timothy Akers with a company later called MerlinBurrows, with Louis De Cordier also involved. Akers described a massive domed structure at Hawara roughly equivalent in scale to the Hagia Sophia in Istanbul. His scans found two large wooden boats near the surface at Hawara, in the style of the Khufu Solar Boat found at Giza, but fully assembled and located on the western end of the complex, inside the flood zone. He described an endless complex of chambers around an enormous central gallery, at least 40 by 100 meters, with structures at 40, 60, 80 and 100 metre depths. And in the middle of that grand central gallery he detected a 40-metre, free-standing, metallic centerpiece object, with a material signature unlike anything he had detected in his career.

files.title: Suppression and Egyptian official pushback
files.body:
Almost everything the sources say about suppression at Hawara traces back to one man's account of one expedition. Louis De Cordier led the 2008 Mataha Expedition, and what he later wrote and said about the aftermath is the spine of the story. Several of the sources retell his account, sometimes with heavy dramatization, and it is worth keeping straight which parts are documented and which parts are a claim being repeated.

The podcast guest who made the viral labyrinth video gives the plainest version. He says the team finished its on-site work in 2008 and 2009 and was ready to release the data. They put on a very small public lecture at Ghent University in Belgium, and in his words no one really attended it. Then they got told to stop. He is careful to say these are De Cordier's words and not his own: De Cordier said he was told to cease any and all discussion or release of information from the Mataha project, and that he and his team members were threatened with national security sanctions from Egypt. The Archaeological Rescue Foundation's Hawara page, written by Trevor Grassi with excerpts from De Cordier, says the same thing in writing. Louis and his team were told not to release the information or tell anyone what they had found, and De Cordier wrote that Dr Zahi Hawass threatened them with national security sanctions.

The article that walks through the rediscovery, under a heading it calls Suppression of Findings, adds the paper trail. The Mataha results were published in the fall 2008 scientific journal of the NRIAG, and the results were exchanged in a public lecture at Ghent University in October 2008 in the presence of the Belgian press. It was not long after that the Secretary General of the Supreme Council of Antiquities put a stop on all communications of the findings, supposedly due to Egyptian National Security sanctions. De Cordier waited two years for the Supreme Council to make the findings public, and by June 2010 it was clear they had no intention of doing so, so he launched his own website. That article ends on a hope rather than a grievance. It says it is hoped that excavations can be launched in future in order to fully explore this hidden gem.

Johanna's video tells it as a shutdown rather than a lecture that happened. She says a public lecture was scheduled where all the information was going to be revealed, free to attend, and that the Secretary General of the Supreme Council of Antiquities shut it down and said they were not going to be approving the release of the findings. She adds that the Egyptian authorities were serious enough that they threatened the French artist and his team with coming after them under an Egyptian security secret act if they released any of the information. Two points of friction there. Johanna calls De Cordier a French artist, while the other sources call him a Belgian artist. She also gives the lecture date as Tuesday the 28th of October 2018, while the article puts the Ghent lecture in October 2008. Johanna performs her anger on camera, calling Hawass a thorn in history and saying she would biff him on the nose, but the underlying claim she is reacting to is De Cordier's.

The Why Files episode is built as entertainment, with a comic sidekick riffing on national security for a 5,000 year old building, and it dramatizes the sequence rather than reporting it fresh. Its factual claim is that Zahi Hawass, Egypt's Secretary General of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, imposed a communication ban on De Cordier's discovery and said it was a matter of national security. That rests on De Cordier's own published account, the same one the other sources use.

The Mataha Expedition's own summary page states the outcome flatly. Further research and excavation have been obstructed by Egyptian authorities, and there has been a near-total blackout by mainstream archaeology and the press.

Two related claims sit alongside it. The Archaeological Rescue Foundation page says that everyone present at the MerlinBurrows scan, including De Cordier, signed a ten year non-disclosure agreement regarding the results. It gives two reasons: partly the intimidation efforts by Hawass to silence the Mataha Expedition, and partly the extreme sensitivity of what was discovered. Separately, in his interview with Johanna, Trevor Grassi says the GPR survey collaborator, Bill Brown's team dug down at the corner of the pyramid and found the original stone corner far underground, showing the pyramid is much bigger than anyone knew. Grassi says that was the final straw that made Zahi kick them out, because they were not supposed to discover how much bigger it really is. That one is Grassi speaking in conversation, not a document.

Grassi also explains why two of the people involved keep their names off the current work. He says he and William Brown have been supporting Lewis from behind the scenes, and that they did not want to get too close to it or get their names on it, because he and Bill both talk about Atlantis and things the ministry does not like.

AncientHistoryX offers a different reason for the quiet around Hawara. It says mainstream archaeology has been cautious about the site for good reason, because past efforts, including Petrie's and later missions, faced the same water issues and bureaucratic hurdles.

The podcast guest is the only source that tries to explain the 2008 silencing as something other than hiding the truth. He says he does not really blame Hawass, and that in his opinion it was a political decision. He grants that hiding the truth is also happening. His reasoning is about how access works. Anything you do in Egypt, whether you are an academic institution or an individual or a funded group, goes through the Council of Antiquities, today the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities. It takes years to get access, and once you have it they control the release of information, so Egypt gets to do the announcing if and when it chooses. He offers the Scan Pyramids project as the example of that pattern. That project used muon detection, the cosmic ray technology, with detectors placed under the ground and in the Grand Gallery at Giza, picking up particles over years to build up enough resolution to tell solid rock from empty space. It found the big void inside the Great Pyramid and also a smaller void at the original main entrance, behind the chevron blocks above the descending passage. When the Scan Pyramids team announced its discoveries on its own initiative, he says, Hawass came out and said this does not exist, there is nothing there, and if there is something there we knew about it already. A couple of years later, when it was time for the press release and the footage, Hawass was the one standing at the podium making the announcement.

The Sphinx video covers an earlier round of the same fight, and it makes its case with archive clips stitched to narration. It says the geologist who redated the Sphinx, Robert Schoch's 1991 seismic findings were presented in an hour long NBC documentary called The Mystery of the Sphinx, watched by more than 30 million people on prime-time television. After West and Schoch revealed those findings, including a room-sized cavity under the left front paw, Egyptian authorities banned them from continuing their research on the Sphinx altogether. The video names Zahi Hawass, whose official title it gives as Minister of Antiquities, as the man responsible, and quotes him calling their research American hallucinations. It then plays a teaser video for the 1996 project at the Sphinx. In it Hawass enters a hole leading into an underground tunnel and exclaims that even Indiana Jones will never dream to be here, saying no one really knows what is inside this tunnel but they are going to open it for the first time. The video says that two years after the project began, Hawass reversed his position, shut down the project, and became adamant that there was nothing under the Sphinx, calling such claims nonsense. Asked about the holes going into the Sphinx, he said they had already looked and there is nothing down there, and that it was probably a shaft put there by treasure hunters. The video's own objection is that no photo or video proof was ever produced to back that up.

The same video walks through the 15 April 2015 event with Graham Hancock. Hawass agreed to participate on one condition, that he would present second, after watching what Hancock presented first. What happened next comes from Hancock's own account, read out by the video. Hawass saw a slide with Robert Bauval's picture on it, became furiously angry, shouted at Hancock, made demeaning comments about Bauval, and said that if Hancock dared to mention a single word about Robert he would walk out and refuse to debate. Then he marched out of the room even before negotiations took place. In the audience question and answer session, a woman asked Hawass about the recent findings at Gobekli Tepe, and the video says he responded as if he had never heard of the site, using hedging phrases like I don't think and in my opinion. The video also plays his response to a question about carbon dating, where he came back with a demand to know why the questioner was using radar in all of their work if they did not believe in it. The narrator presents that line as the thing that should discredit anything Hawass has ever said, and reads his body language as flustered. That verdict belongs to the narrator. It is not something the footage documents.

One more cluster of official pushback sits at Giza rather than Hawara, and it runs the other way. The news report on the Khafre Project, the Italian-led study by Filippo Biondi and Corrado Malanga that announced a vast underground city on 23 March 2025, says the claims have drawn sharp criticism from experts. Zahi Hawass rejected the claims and asserted that they have no scientific basis, and he noted that Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities had not authorized any work around the Khafre pyramid. Former Egyptian Minister of Antiquities Mamdouh al-Damaty dismissed the claims as utterly baseless, pointing out that decades of archaeological research have found no evidence to support the underground city theory. Egyptologist Hussein Abdel-Basir criticized the study for lacking proper scientific standards. He highlighted that no peer-reviewed paper has accompanied the claims, which were presented at a press conference, and he said the researchers' claims seem more aligned with conspiracy theories than scientific inquiry.

files.title: Underground tunnels and features around the Giza Plateau
files.body:
The oldest of these claims comes from a decade-long clearing project on the plateau. The Sphinx video, the one that opens with the 1923 discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb, quotes Hamilton M. Wright, whose team said it had found a large underground ancient subway system used by the ancient Egyptians 5,000 years ago. In Wright's words, it passes beneath the causeway leading between the second pyramid and the Sphinx. From the subway, he said, they unearthed a series of shafts leading down more than 125 feet, with roomy quarters and side chambers.

Written accounts of tunnels there are much older. About 800 years after Herodotus, the Syrian philosopher Iamblichus wrote of an underground tunnel system that could be reached through the body of the Sphinx. He said galleries were cut out in the belly of the Sphinx leading to the subterranean part of the Great Pyramid, and that these galleries were so artfully crisscrossed that anyone setting out without a guide would inevitably return to the starting point.

The same video argues that the accepted date for the Sphinx rests on thin evidence. The Great Pyramid is widely accepted as the tomb of Khufu, yet no mummy of anyone, Khufu included, has ever been found inside it. Supporters of the standard timeline point to a well-preserved statue of Khafre and say its face matches the face on the Sphinx.
