The video measures one angle on both faces, running from the corner of the lips to the corner of the eye, and says it is almost double on the Sphinx compared with Khafre's actual face. It reads that as proof the two faces belong to different people. Then there is the Inventory Stela, discovered by a French archaeologist in Egypt during the 1850s. Inscribed into that stone is a record of the Sphinx being repaired by the Pharaoh Khufu after it was struck by lightning. Khufu was Khafre's father and was supposed to have been dead by the time the Sphinx was built, so the stela cuts against the timeline.

The video also spends time on how the Sphinx was made. The pyramids were built block by block. The Sphinx was not. It was sculpted directly out of the bedrock, from a single piece of limestone. The massive limestone blocks taken out of the ground around it were then reused to build a nearby temple complex. We know that because the geological layers inside the blocks of the temple complex match the geological layers of the walls around the Sphinx. Some of those blocks measure 30 feet long, 10 feet high and 12 feet wide, and weigh about 200 tons each. The builders are said to have moved them with nothing more than ropes, pulleys and ramps.

On the question of holes, the video says it is well documented that there are holes going into the Sphinx. One sits on top of the head and is currently sealed shut with concrete. One is covered by a block, with a tunnel clearly leading under the Sphinx. One is on the back, and Zahi Hawass himself is on video looking down into it.

Two more items from that video are worth separating from what they are attached to. The first is an account from the 1830s, only a few years after the Sphinx was dug out of the ground, when a team of French engineers exploring the grounds around it apparently discovered a doorway leading underground. Shortly after, the account goes, they were confronted by shadowy figures who forced them to stop their research altogether. The video presents this as one story in a long line of rumours about an Egyptian mafia controlling the flow of information, and it offers no documentation for the confrontation. The second is the ground between the paws. Today the ground around the Sphinx is largely flat bedrock, except directly between the two front paws, where floorboards have been placed over what seem to be tiles. Those tiles were not carved into the bedrock. They were placed at the same elevation as the rest of the ground around them. The floorboards have been there since the 1800s, when the Sphinx was dug out. The video then asks whether the tiles could be the roof of a chamber under the Sphinx, and whether that chamber could hold an archive from Atlantis. The Atlantis reading is the video's speculation, phrased as a question. What sits underneath it is the floorboards, the tiles and their elevation.

Johanna comes at the tunnels from a different direction. She says she was researching an underground tunnel system and watched a video by Ben from the YouTube channel Uncharted X about the tunnel system in and around the Giza Plateau. From that she reports that the tunnel system at Giza is connected to Saqqara, about 8 miles away, and that you could walk through from the Sphinx to the pyramid to Saqqara. She says it is all connected and it is unexplored.

The Wikipedia entry on the Hall of Records covers the same ground and traces where the ideas came from. It describes the Hall of Records as a purported ancient library claimed to exist underground near the Great Sphinx of Giza in Egypt. It notes that Pliny the Elder, a Roman author of the first century AD, reported that the people living near Giza in his time believed the Great Sphinx was hollow and contained the tomb of a king named Harmais. Medieval Islamic legends asserted there were subterranean passages beneath the pyramids there. Giovanni Battista Caviglia, who excavated at Giza in the early nineteenth century, believed a network of subterranean passages linked together all the Giza pyramids. On Cayce, the entry says he stated the Giza hall lay somewhere between the sphinx and the Nile River, with an entrance near the sphinx's right paw. The geophysicist Thomas Dobecki, working on the 1991 survey, argued that seismography showed a possibly man-made chamber under the sphinx's right paw. When the surveys turned up no sign of the hall, adherents shifted attention to the water shaft, also called the Osiris shaft, a subterranean tomb west of the sphinx cut during the Late Period, around 664 to 332 BC. They argued the tomb might be connected to the hall. The shaft was first recorded by the Egyptologist Selim Hassan in the 1930s but could not be fully explored because it was flooded. The entry's verdict is flat. Nothing matching Cayce's description has ever been found.

The most recent round of claims is about the Pyramid of Khafre, which sits in the center of the Great Pyramids of Giza. The fact-check article that went through them describes the purported discovery as five identical structures near the Khafre Pyramid's base, linked by pathways, and eight deep vertical wells descending 648 meters underground. Users shared it on X, Instagram and TikTok, with some calling it a vast underground city. One YouTube video sharing the claim stood at over 35,000 views as of that article's writing. A tweet from an account called Leonard Murphy Personal Account referenced a team of Corrado Malanga, Armando Mei, Filippo Biondi and Nicole Ciccolo, and Synthetic Aperture Radar scanning of the Khafre Pyramid. The article's finding is that there is no evidence to support the claim of vast underground structures beneath the Khafre Pyramid, and that no credible news outlets or scientific publications have reported on it. Infowars founder Alex Jones shared a version of the same claim on X.

The article also tracks what people built on top of the claim. The Reese Report theorized that the alleged discovery supported the idea that the pyramids were built as a sort of ancient power plant rather than as tombs. It suggested the cylindrical wells could be conduits for energy or sound waves, and that the cubic structures might serve as energy storage or stabilization units, akin to components in a large-scale weapon or generator. The Khafre Project hopes to plan an excavation to learn more about the alleged underground structure, though the article notes that history shows such approval is very difficult to get. On the method, it quotes NASA: SAR is a type of active data collection where an instrument sends out a pulse of energy and then records the amount of that energy reflected back after it interacts with Earth. The article's own read is that the research alludes to fringe theories, and that this aligns with Malanga's well-documented interest in UFO and alien abduction research as well as with Dunn's power plant theory.

Two of that article's checks are worth keeping in full. One of the most popular images shared in support of the claim, showing a cross section of the pyramid and the alleged structures, was generated using artificial intelligence. Uploading the image to the AI-detection platform Hive Moderation returned a 99.9% chance the image was AI-generated. And the Khafre Project itself does not appear to exist beyond a YouTube channel run by a woman named Nicole Ciccolo, who posts frequent unsubstantiated theories about the pyramids. No website or further information about the organization could be found.

The same article looked into the event where the findings were supposedly revealed. Details of it, such as how many people attended or who they were, were unknown, and the press release was not publicly available. A Facebook post claimed to share the main points of a presentation that allegedly took place there. Advertisements for the event on Facebook and on a website for Archeoares, an Italian museum group, claimed the event sold out. Archeoares' social media pages share frequent photos of their events, but none from the purported Khafre Project conference were publicly available. Filippo Biondi did post about it on LinkedIn, saying that during the event they explored the Giza Plateau and the application of a technique he developed called Doppler Tomography, generated through Synthetic Aperture Radar. Biondi did not immediately respond to inquiries about the claim.

The news report on the study gives the researchers' own version, and its numbers do not line up with the fact-check article's. It describes a study titled the Khafre Project led by the Italian researchers Filippo Biondi of the University of Strathclyde and Corrado Malanga of the University of Pisa. The researchers suggested the hidden city extends over 6,500 feet, far larger than the pyramids themselves. Malanga and Biondi used pulse radar technology to generate high-resolution images of the subsurface. The method is similar to the sonar used for mapping the ocean floor, detecting underground features by sending radar waves into the ground and analyzing the reflected signals. The report alleges the discovery of eight vertical structures extending over 2,100 feet beneath the pyramids, and additional unidentified structures potentially lying at depths of 4,000 feet. The claims suggest a complex network of vertical cylindrical wells was discovered that could challenge our understanding of the area's archaeological significance. So the eight wells are given as 648 meters deep in one account and as over 2,100 feet in the other, with a further set of structures at 4,000 feet named only in the second. Both figures are on the record and neither source reconciles them.

The strongest technical objection in this material comes from Lawrence Conyers, a ground-penetrating radar researcher at the University of Denver. He called the idea of an underground city a huge exaggeration. His point is about the equipment rather than the site. He emphasised that the technology used cannot penetrate that deeply, and suggested any findings would likely be small structures rather than a massive city.

files.title: Water erosion on the Sphinx
files.body:
The video that walks through Robert Schoch's 1991 work at Giza quotes the NBC documentary The Mystery of the Sphinx directly. Schoch looked at the erosion patterns on the walls around the Sphinx and found they looked nothing like sand and wind erosion. They looked identical to extreme water erosion, meaning rainfall runoff. His evidence is the distinctive joint patterns in the limestone. You do not see the same type of joints in wind-induced weathering, he says, and what is on those walls is a textbook example of what happens to a limestone wall when rain beats down on it for thousands of years. He also heads off the obvious alternative. Nile River flooding would give a very different geological signature on the rock, because floods come up from the bottom. The pattern he is looking at is rainfall runoff coming from above.

John Anthony West's contribution is a story about testing that reading on someone with no stake in it. Through friends he got an introduction to a very well-known Oxford geologist, and he asked whether a geologist could tell weathering by water from weathering by wind and sand on the basis of a clear photograph alone. The answer, cautiously expressed, was that as a general rule yes. So West played a trick. He took a photograph of the Sphinx, masked off the head and paws, and asked what was responsible for the weathering. The geologist looked at it for a moment and said unquestionably water. Then West stripped the masking tape off.

From there West and Schoch draw the date. Given the level of water erosion that exists, the Sphinx must go back to a time when the area was very wet with heavy precipitation instead of desert. The last time conditions fit that description was around the end of the last ice age, roughly 12,000 years ago, when huge climatic changes put a lot of moisture into the air and it came down as precipitation and huge thunderstorms. West states the implication flatly. Proof that the Sphinx precedes dynastic Egypt by many thousands of years means there was a sophisticated civilization at some point in the distant past.

The same video lines up two other dates with that one. The dating of Gobekli Tepe and the Sphinx's proposed older age both land at the end of the last ice age, and that is also the date Plato gives for the destruction of Atlantis.

The Osireion material comes from the Why Files episode, which delivers it at speed as narration rather than reporting it. It says the same weathering appears on the Osireion at Abydos, that its massive red granite blocks are cut with a precision modern engineers struggle to replicate, and that constant water fills the lower chambers and cannot be pumped out, which the episode reads as a site designed for water. The episode also cites Strabo, who stated explicitly that the Osireion and the labyrinth shared the same builder, a king he called Ismandes.

files.title: Pre-flood origin theories and lost civilizations
files.body:
Two of the sources argue for a lost civilization, and one describes where that argument came from. Keeping those apart matters here, because the same names turn up on both sides.

The Sphinx video, the one that opens with the 1923 discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb, builds its case toward Edgar Cayce. It says Cayce claimed that Atlantis, the mythical advanced civilization which sank into the ocean, was actually real, and that the full history of Atlantis would be revealed on scrolls located inside the Hall of Records under the Sphinx. The video then heads off the obvious objection by going back to where the Atlantis story starts. It traces the myth to the writings of the Greek philosopher Plato, who described Atlantis as an advanced ancient civilization that existed 9,000 years before his own time and was founded by beings that were half god and half human. The video points out that Plato never said the story was not real. He said he heard it through conversations he had with various poets and priests. One of those was with the Greek lawmaker Solon, who told Plato about going to Egypt and meeting one of the Egyptian high priests. In Solon's account, as the video tells it, the priest laughed at the Greek version of history and explained that there had been many devastations in the long history of the world, that the Earth had been repopulated many times over the course of millions of years, that the Greeks only remembered the last one, and that the Egyptians still held the records of the earlier histories the Greeks had lost.

The same video uses Gobekli Tepe in Turkey as its answer to the question of where the evidence for such an early culture is. It says the site was discovered by accident, when a shepherd stumbled over a bunch of old looking stones sticking out of a hillside, and that for many years it was assumed to be nothing more than a medieval cemetery. Excavation found large circular structures supported by massive stone pillars, each weighing 7 to 10 tons and standing 18 feet high. Most mysteriously, the video says, the whole thing seems to have been deliberately buried in the ground all at once, as if to preserve it or hide it. Carbon dating of materials at the site puts construction at around 12,000 years ago, which means it predates ancient Sumeria, the invention of writing, and Stonehenge by more than 6,000 years. The video gives that gap a shape a listener can hold. There was about as much time between the building of Gobekli Tepe and the building of Stonehenge as there was between Stonehenge and today. That makes Gobekli Tepe the oldest known megalithic site in the world. Many of the pillars have 3D animals carved directly out of the stone with extreme precision and detail. Many of the tops also appear to have faces on them, which is why the pillars are believed to represent stylized versions of human beings.

The Why Files episode runs a similar argument through the labyrinth itself. Its cold open puts the claim as a condition. If the priests were telling the truth, the Egyptians did not build the labyrinth. They found it. Later the narration is blunter. The Egyptian priests said the labyrinth was not built by the pharaoh as a burial tomb. It was built by a much older civilization as a library, because those ancient people needed a place to store their knowledge before they were wiped out in a great flood. The episode then goes to Egyptian texts. The Egyptians called the pre-flood era Zep Tepi, or the first time. The Pyramid Texts talk about it repeatedly, and the Turin King List carries dates and durations for divine rulers who reigned for thousands of years before the human pharaohs. The episode is careful to state the other reading straight away. Mainstream Egyptology calls this symbolic, and says the gods represent concepts rather than beings. It then turns to the Temple of Horus at Edfu, where the Edfu building texts span over 300 feet of wall space and describe the temple's construction on foundations from an earlier structure that existed before the flood. Those texts reference beings called the Shebtiu, followers of Horus who arrived after a great cataclysm destroyed their homeland, and they mention seven sages who came with them from an island swallowed by the sea. What the texts say these beings brought is knowledge of astronomy, architecture, mathematics and medicine. It is worth saying that the Why Files is a scripted show with a comic sidekick and a sponsor read in the first minute, so the material arrives performed. The claims about Zep Tepi and Edfu are its narration, not a citation to a paper.

The Why Files also gives its own version of Cayce. In the 1930s, it says, Cayce described another archive. He was a trance medium who delivered over 14,000 documented readings across 43 years, and he diagnosed medical conditions for patients he had never met, conditions he had no training to identify. According to Cayce, an advanced civilization was destroyed around 10,000 BC, but there were survivors, and they scattered to Egypt, the Yucatan and the Bahamas, bringing technology and knowledge with them. The episode says Cayce was specific about that technology. It mentions sound waves used for construction, and acoustic levitation.

Johanna, on her own channel, offers the same shape as a personal theory and flags it as hers. She says the theory she is running with now is that around 10,000 years ago there was a huge deluge, and you got the Younger Dryas comet, and the world basically turned to crap. What she imagines people doing is going to ground, building safety underground, because nobody knew when the sky was next going to fall in. You would try to preserve your family and your evidence and everything you have underground. She thinks this happened not just in Egypt but all over.

The Wikipedia article on the Hall of Records covers the same names from the other direction, tracing where the idea came from rather than whether it is true. It says the concept originated with claims made by Edgar Cayce, an American who claimed to be clairvoyant and was a forerunner of the New Age movement, and that he said in the 1930s that refugees from Atlantis built the Hall of Records at Giza to preserve their knowledge. It adds that in the 1990s Cayce's claims about the Hall of Records became conflated with two other fringe hypotheses about the origin and age of the Giza monuments, the sphinx water erosion hypothesis and the Orion correlation theory.

The precursors are laid out in some detail. The belief that ancient records were stored at Giza derives from medieval Islamic traditions about a legendary king of Egypt named Surid ibn Salhouk, who is said to have ruled Egypt before the flood described in the Book of Genesis and to have built the Great Pyramid of Giza to preserve his society's knowledge in the event of that flood. The Surid legend was translated several times into European languages, beginning with seventeenth century translations by John Greaves and Pierre Vattier, and it became a major influence on later fringe beliefs about ancient Egypt. Ignatius Donnelly, the Atlantis theorist, argued that Atlantis influenced numerous civilizations around the world, including ancient Egypt, before being destroyed in a catastrophe that inspired the biblical flood myth. Closer still to the Hall of Records are the works of H. C. Randall-Stevens and Harvey Spencer Lewis. In several publications beginning in the late 1920s, Randall-Stevens asserted that the Egyptians built the Giza pyramids and the sphinx after the destruction of Atlantis, and that beneath the Giza Plateau lay a complex of subterranean passages and temples where inductees into the Egyptians' mystical wisdom received instruction and underwent initiation. Randall-Stevens said he was channeling his information from the spirits of Egyptian initiates. Lewis said his assertions were based on records from his esoteric organization, the Ancient and Mystical Order Rosae Crucis. The author Jason Colavito argues that both men were imitating Masonic legends about the ancient origins of Masonic rites, with possible influence from the Islamic legends about the pyramids.

On Cayce himself, the article says he was the first person to use the term "Hall of Records". During the first half of the twentieth century he gave thousands of readings, meaning statements made while in a trance, concerning particular people. Some of the subjects of what he called life readings had, he claimed, lived in Atlantis in their past lives, and so he described Atlantis in detail. His characterization of Atlantis owed much to Donnelly, although he said it possessed advanced technologies that were absent from Donnelly's version. The two accounts of his output do not match. The Why Files counts over 14,000 documented readings across 43 years and stresses the medical diagnoses of patients he had never met. The Wikipedia article says thousands of readings across the first half of the century and describes them as trance statements about particular people. Both are here, and neither number is checked against the other.

The last stretch of the article deals with what the idea turned into. The authors Adrian Gilbert and Robert Bauval put forward the Orion correlation theory, which argues that the monuments at Giza were arranged according to stellar alignments from several thousand years before the conventional date of their construction. Hancock, Bauval and John Anthony West all advocated these claims and attracted wide publicity, and it was West who had initially convinced Schoch to study the erosion of the sphinx. Hancock and Bauval also implied that future finds at Giza could have a transformative impact on the world, and they connected those transformative events with the impending beginning of the third millennium and with the astrological Age of Aquarius. Enthusiasm over the Hall of Records waned toward the end of the 1990s, as the predicted window of time for its discovery passed and as mainstream academic criticisms of the claims about Giza came to be more widely aired. Colavito writes that beliefs about the Hall of Records are motivated by the idea that seeking out physical evidence of Atlantis or some other lost civilization would somehow prove that the spiritual values embodied by occult and New Age groups were objectively true. In his words the search became a cudgel to be used against doubt, since the possibility that physical proof could be found removed the temptation to question the otherwise outlandish claims believers were asked to accept.

files.title: The Hawara rescue project and the water threat
files.body:
Trevor Grassi joined Johanna's video with new information about the Hawara pyramid and about what he calls a rescue archaeology project there. Hawara sits in the Fayum region of Egypt, and it is the historically documented site of the lost labyrinth of Egypt. Johanna lays that much out herself at the top of the video, before Trevor comes on the call. Most of what follows is the two of them sharing a screen and reading a planning document out loud, so the excitement in the video belongs to them. The document itself lives on the Archaeological Rescue Foundation's website.

The project is officially approved, and it has a short-term plan, a medium-term plan and a long-term plan for Hawara. Trevor says the long-term plan is where the full rerouting of the canal away from the site now sits, because rerouting is a lot more expensive. The short-term plan is to patch the canal first. He says he originally expected the complete reroute to come at the start.

The institutions he names include two British universities, the GEM, which is the Grand Egyptian Museum, and Cairo University, along with a group he calls NAG that is led by Dr Abbas. A foundation called Athanatos is funding parts of the work, and so is Lewis's new foundation. Trevor says the funding is already secured for the first couple of project seasons, and that multiple universities and sponsors have committed support. He also says divers have already gone in to clear stones and document the interior. That part is second hand in his own telling. He says it has happened supposedly, and that no report has been released yet.

The first year of the rescue plan, the short-term block, covers securing baseline data, legal governance, website communication, drone photogrammetry, LiDAR scanning of the pyramid exterior, cleaning the entrance shaft, diver exploration, a geophysical survey, and borehole drilling, especially across the labyrinth's south zone.

The one-to-five-year block is mostly about water. It covers fixing the water and drainage issues, lining the canal with concrete, reinforcing shafts, installing pumps, and building a watchtower, offices and visitor facilities. The long-term block covers a visitor center, digital legacy and education programs, and research training for local youth. Trevor points to Bill Brown's earlier Hawara project, running roughly from 2007 to 2009, which helped 50 different students earn their master's degrees. He says a similar student program is planned again.

The Archaeological Rescue Foundation is run by the host's collaborators, and Trevor says it aims to prioritise which archaeological sites to support. Its website, archaeologicalrescue.org, hosts a Hawara project page that compiles the past scanning projects and then, at the bottom, the newly released planning document. Reading from the very end of that document, Johanna points out the authority statement. It says all activities will be under the authority of Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities and the Supreme Council of Antiquities.

Both of them speculate about what a successful excavation would mean. The host says it could double Egypt's tourism industry, and that getting inside would force a rewriting of aspects of human history. That is conversation on a live call, not a finding. The same tourism claim appears in a firmer form in the foundation's own document, which suggests a discovery of Hawara's scale could potentially double the scale of Egypt's tourism industry.

On the water itself, the Wikipedia article on Hawara gives the plain measurement. The entrance to the pyramid is today flooded to a depth of 6 metres, as a result of waters from the Abdul Wahbi canal, an offshoot of the Bahr Yussef canal. That canal flows around two sides of the site and passes within 30 metres of the pyramid.

The Mataha Expedition's own page adds what the water is doing. Rising saline groundwater is actively eroding what remains of the labyrinth, which makes preservation an urgent priority. The page says the Mataha Expedition's mission is far from over, and that further scientific research, international awareness and urgent conservation efforts are needed to uncover the full scale of the labyrinth and prevent its irreversible destruction.

The comment thread under the Ancient Origins article on the expedition is where readers ask whether anything has actually been done. One commenter says that as far as they know, no actions have been taken to drain the location of the groundwater. The same commenter says they believe draining is nearly impossible, because it is the groundwater table and it is fed by the Nile. They also note that a canal now runs over the supposed location of the labyrinth. Another comment says the roof of the building is under several feet of sand and is almost completely under water because of the groundwater table, and adds that, because of that sand and groundwater, the site is luckily not going to be vandalised soon.

The AncientHistoryX article reports that official excavations have kicked off at the Hawara site in Faiyum, Egypt. The goal of the mission is to locate and document any surviving remains of the Labyrinth. The article says the high-water table from the nearby Bahr Wahbi canal has always been the big obstacle, as noted in earlier Polish and Egyptian missions and in groundwater studies. It credits recent planning by the Mataha Foundation and the Archaeological Rescue Foundation, including detailed master plans for preservation. Those plans include digging diversion canals and, in the article's own wording, fauna planted to reduce the water to a manageable level so that it can be pumped from the site. The article calls the new excavation the logical next step, ground-truthing the anomalies before rising groundwater does more damage. Its author claims that if they confirm even part of the Labyrinth's layout, it could rewrite what we know about Middle Kingdom temple architecture and Amenemhat III's vision.

The foundation's own plan-and-cost section is more specific about the sequence. Eventually the entire canal must be rerouted around the entire site. Initially it must at least be patched with cement, and grasses must be planted in the northern areas, because their root structures will divert much of the water flowing in from the north. Once that constant inflow stops, the water can be drained and the structures entered. Many chambers will need excavation of sand or mud, which the plan says will require a large digging team for many seasons, plus archaeological professionals and security. Once the structures can be entered, the plan proposes creating a perfect photogrammetric model of the entire complex exactly as it is, using precise equipment to measure each chamber and 360 degree cameras to map their surfaces, without touching a single item. The cost, the plan says, will be well into the millions, and the project will last for many years to come. It also states that lowering the water table too far could affect local agriculture, so the water needs of the local farmers will be taken into account.

files.title: Other underground sites and personal updates
files.body:
This is the material that sits around the edges of the Hawara story. Some of it is Johanna talking about other holes in the ground, and some of it is housekeeping from the people involved.

Johanna reaches for two other underground sites while explaining why she thinks people went to ground after a catastrophe. The first is the underground city found in Turkey, which she mentions in passing as another example. The second is on her doorstep. The Chislehurst Caves are a 25 mile underground cave system near her home in South London. Her point about them is that you would never know they were there unless you knew they were there, which she says is the whole point of a secret underground cave system. It is open to the public. The traditional story is that the Saxons were the first people to carve it out, and she pushes back on that in her own words. She says it is a pretty random thing for Saxons to do, and she wonders whether the caves are in fact much older, and whether they connect to a time when humans were trying to get underground to survive. She adds one piece of recent history that she thinks makes the point. During the Second World War, thousands of people in London lived in the Chislehurst Caves. They slept there and lived there because the bombing made their houses unsafe. Her conclusion is that if it happened then, it could have happened many times before.

At the end of that same video she runs through her own year. It is 2022, and she says she has trips planned. She is going to Egypt in September with fellow YouTuber Ancient Architects, and she says there are still one or two spaces left, with the information in the description box. The name of the channel comes through garbled in the transcript audio. She also says she has special private access to Chernobyl in Ukraine, and plans to take viewers creeping around it with her, because she loves abandoned historical places. Then comes the merchandise. She has designed a fake band t-shirt called The Copper Chisels. The joke came from a running gag on tour in Egypt, where everything they saw prompted the same question about how it was made, and the same answer: copper chisels. If you do not know the ancient history reference, she says, it just looks like a cool retro band t-shirt. She is also selling a copy of the design of her own ancient history tattoo, which is on her arm and shows the Pyramids of Giza, the constellation of Leo, and the blue lotus flower.

The other personal note is Johanna's opening to the impromptu interview video. She had a baby roughly six months before recording, which is why she had not been making videos for the last six or seven months. She corrects herself on the number as she says it.

The Archaeological Rescue Foundation's Hawara page carries a running list of updates, newest first, and two of them are scheduling and release news. Update number three, dated July 21, announces the release of HAWARA RISING PART TWO, headlined as excavation revealing a megalithic wall of the Lost Labyrinth of Egypt. Trevor Grassi describes what is in it. There is on-site footage from his Egypt tour with Mohamed Ibrahim in March, when excavations at Hawara first began. There is an interview he recorded with Louis De Cordier in Italy, in which De Cordier gives insights into the coordination of the new Hawara Mission. There is an update from the week before with Yousef Sayed Bdaway, carrying new photos of the megalithic wall uncovered by the first few months of excavation. The same update invites readers to join Louis De Cordier and Trevor Grassi at Hawara from February 1 to 4, 2027, with full tour details on the foundation's site.

Update number two, dated June 9th, is the earlier one. It says that on the 21st of June, Trevor Grassi of the Archaeological Rescue Foundation will be meeting in Bologna, Italy with Louis De Cordier, Dr Filippo Biondi and several others who are helping Mission Hawara to move forward.

files.title: Labyrinth symbolism and cross-cultural origins
files.body:
The word 'labyrinth' was not the builders' word. The Historic Mysteries article is careful about this: the builders of the Egyptian complex did not consider it a labyrinth in the modern sense of the word. Herodotus named it as such, after the legendary Greek labyrinth built by Daedalus for King Minos of Crete, where in Greek mythology the minotaur dwelt at the heart of an elaborate maze of tunnels. So the name arrives with Herodotus and carries his cultural frame, not the Egyptians'.

The same article argues that labyrinths were not initially intended to be confusing, merely expansive and complex. It traces the original word to 'labrys', the ceremonial axe used by the Minoan civilization, and says the thing so named was more likely a sprawling palace complex. It backs this with what survives on Crete. Frescoes on the island depict young men acrobatically jumping over charging bulls for sport, and the article says it is not inconceivable to see the origin of the minotaur myth in such daredevil stunts. Minoan palaces were commonly large and had a central open area where events like that could take place, which would put men fighting a giant bull at the heart of the labyrinth. That last step is the article's own suggestion about how the myth may have formed, offered as a possibility rather than as an established fact.

Beyond Crete and Egypt, the article notes that what we call labyrinths have been built throughout history and for many reasons. Malevolent spirits may have been trapped in prehistoric labyrinths, or ritual dances may have taken place in them. Many Roman and Christian labyrinths are found at building entrances, where the design may similarly have been used to ward off evil.

For the cross-cultural picture the article leans on Carl Schuster and Edmund Carpenter, whose 1996 study of signs and symbols, Patterns that Connect: Social Symbolism in Ancient and Tribal Art, ISBN 9780810963269, presents various forms of the labyrinth and suggests various possible intentions behind their construction. One suggestion is that some could form a sacred processional path to the home of a sacred ancestor, and the article compares this to some theories about the Nazca Lines in Peru, adding that the path might also depict the ancestor himself. In some Indian cultures, it says, the labyrinth is regarded as a sacred symbol, a helpful ancestor, and a divinity, which may preserve that original meaning: the ultimate ancestor, evoked by two continuous lines connecting the living to the dead.

Schuster also noticed a second motif running across cultures, the labyrinth as a shelter for a trickster. In India the demon Ravana rules over labyrinths. Among the Sumatran Bataks, the trickster Djonaha dwells in a labyrinth. For Europeans it is often a cage, built to trap whatever monster is hidden at its heart.

files.title: Everything else
files.body: One loose fact sits outside the other groupings, and it is about what Hawara looks like today. Johanna, opening her interview with Trevor Grassi, gives a short orientation for viewers who do not know the site. She says that nowadays there is nothing but sand outside the pyramid of Hawara, and that the pyramid itself looks a little bit sorry for itself, because it is a mud-brick pyramid that has kind of melted into the desert. That is the whole of it. Nothing in her description adds a measurement or a date to the point.

disputes.claim: There is a direct contradiction between the established archaeological consensus that the Labyrinth was destroyed and quarried away and the data from modern geophysical scans which indicate a massive, intact structure still exists underground.

case_for.heading: The scans say something is still down there
case_for.text: Start with where the Labyrinth sits. It is an underground structure, so whatever survives of it lies below the surface rather than standing in the open where stone robbers work first. Modern geophysical scanning of that ground came back showing a large structure still in place. The part this side leans hardest on is the match. What the instruments picked up lines up with the way ancient writers described the Labyrinth. On this reading, the scans are not showing an anomaly that needs a name. They are showing the building the old descriptions were describing, in the place it was said to be. It has to be said plainly that this is the whole of the case as the corpus supplies it. Nobody has opened the ground to look. There is no dig, no photograph from inside, no measurement of a wall anyone has touched. The argument stands on the scan reading and on the fit with the ancient accounts.

case_against.heading: The consensus says it was quarried away
case_against.text: The established archaeological position is that the Labyrinth did not survive. It was destroyed, and its stone was carried off and reused, which is why there is no building left to find. That position is stated in the corpus as the settled view of the field. What the corpus does not carry is the case behind it. No excavation report is supplied. No archaeologist is named. Nothing is offered that shows the quarrying happening, and nothing is offered that explains what the geophysical scans were picking up if the building is gone. Anyone weighing this side is being asked to take the consensus on its standing in the field, because the evidence for it has not been put in front of them here.

disputes.claim: There is a tension between the official narrative of the Sphinx's origin (4,500 years old, built by Khafre) and the alternative theory presented (12,000 years old, built by a lost civilization), which is supported by geological evidence, historical accounts, and the existence of other ancient sites like Göbekli Tepe.

case_for.heading: Twelve thousand years old, and older than Egypt
case_for.text: The alternative position is that the Sphinx is roughly twelve thousand years old and was cut by a civilisation that came before dynastic Egypt. Three kinds of support are claimed for it. Geological evidence about how the stone has worn is said to point to a far earlier date than the pharaohs. Historical accounts are said to preserve a memory of an older origin. And Gobekli Tepe is offered as proof that people were already building monumental stone sites long before anyone thought they could. That is the shape of the argument. The corpus does not supply what is inside it. No geologist is named. No weathering measurement or date is given. Nothing is quoted from the historical accounts, and nothing about Gobekli Tepe is set out beyond the fact that it exists. The case is asserted here rather than shown.

case_against.heading: Khafre's monument, about 4,500 years old
case_against.text: The official position is the one taught and published: the Sphinx is around four and a half thousand years old and was built by Khafre. It ties the monument to a known king, a known dynasty, and the rest of the Giza plateau around it. The corpus carries no case for it. There is no inscription quoted, no excavation cited, no Egyptologist named, and no dating method described. The dating is present as the accepted narrative and nothing more, so on the evidence supplied here it rests on the authority of the field rather than on anything a reader can check.

disputes.claim: A tension exists in the behavior of Zahi Hawass, who is depicted publicly dismissing the existence of significant structures under the Sphinx as "hallucinations" and banning researchers, while also being filmed exploring underground tunnels himself before shutting down his own project and denying anything is there.

case_for.heading: He looked, then said there was nothing to look at
case_for.text: The behaviour is the argument. In public, Zahi Hawass dismissed the idea of significant structures under the Sphinx as hallucinations, and he barred researchers who wanted to test it. At the same time he was filmed underground himself, moving through tunnels at the site. The one hard detail the corpus supplies is what happened next. Two years after the project began, Hawass reversed his position, shut the project down, and denied there was anything under the Sphinx, calling the claims nonsense. Those two years are what this side keeps coming back to. A man who thought there was nothing there does not run an underground project for two years before announcing that there is nothing there. That single reversal is also the whole of the supplied evidence. Hawass's own account of why he closed the project is not in the corpus, so the reasoning behind the reversal has never been put on the record here.

case_against.heading: No case supplied on the other side
case_against.text: There is no counter-case in the corpus. Nothing is supplied that explains the reversal in ordinary terms, and nothing is supplied from Hawass or anyone working with him giving a reason for closing the project. No funding record, no permit, no interview, no statement of his own is offered. Whatever the innocent reading of his behaviour might be, the corpus does not make it, so this side sits empty on the evidence available here.

disputes.claim: A tension exists between the presentation of modern remote sensing data and geological analysis suggesting an older, more complex history for Egypt, and the official archaeological narrative which is alleged to suppress or ignore this data.

case_for.heading: The data points older, and it gets ignored
case_for.text: The position is that modern remote sensing and geological analysis of Egyptian sites keep pointing to a past that is older and more complicated than the accepted timeline allows, and that official archaeology will not engage with it. On this reading the instruments are doing their job and the results are being left on the shelf. The corpus does not supply what the position needs. No scan is described, no survey is cited, and no geologist is named. No specific instance of a paper being blocked, a permit being pulled, or a finding being buried is given. The claim about suppression is made without a single documented case behind it here.

case_against.heading: The official archaeological narrative
case_against.text: The other side holds that the accepted picture of Egyptian history is the one the evidence supports, and that nothing is being suppressed. The corpus carries no case for it. No archaeologist responds. No reanalysis of the sensing data is supplied. Nothing is offered showing how the profession has handled these results, or why it reads them differently. This side is named in the dispute and left unargued in the material at hand.

disputes.claim: A tension exists between what is reportedly known about the Labyrinth's existence and scale from historical texts and modern scans, and what remains unknown and speculative due to a stated prohibition on excavation.

case_for.heading: The existence and scale are established
case_for.text: This side holds that the basic facts about the Labyrinth are already settled. Historical texts describe the building, and modern scanning of the ground has found something answering to it, so the argument is that its existence and its size are known rather than guessed at. The corpus supplies nothing behind that. No text is quoted. No scan result, depth, or dimension is given. No surveyor or writer is named. The confidence is stated in the corpus without the readings or the passages that would let anyone else check it.

case_against.heading: Nobody has opened the ground
case_against.text: The counter-position is that all of this stays speculative while excavation is prohibited. Texts and remote readings can suggest what is down there. Only digging can show it, and the digging has not been allowed. Until it is, the size, the layout, and the contents remain claims about a building nobody has seen. The corpus supplies no evidence for this side either. The prohibition itself is stated and never documented. There is no named authority behind it, no date, no ruling, and no account of who asked and was refused.

disputes.claim: A tension is present within the alternative narrative itself regarding the primary location of a lost civilization's archive, contrasting the well-known "Hall of Records" theory at Giza with the proposal that the Labyrinth at Hawara is the more logical site.

case_for.heading: Hawara is the more logical site
case_for.text: The argument for Hawara starts with what the site already is. The Hawara pyramid sits in the Fayum region, and it is the historically documented location of the lost Labyrinth of Egypt. That is not a proposal about Hawara. It is what the record says the place was. So if a lost civilisation left an archive anywhere, this side says the sensible place to look is the one building the ancient sources actually describe as vast, chambered, and full of rooms. On top of that, Trevor Grassi says he has new information about the Hawara pyramid and about a rescue archaeology project there. That new information is the freshest part of the case and it rests on Grassi alone. The corpus gives his claim and no one corroborating it. It is worth being straight about the gap as well. What is supplied ties Hawara to the Labyrinth. Nothing supplied ties the Labyrinth to an archive.

case_against.heading: The Hall of Records at Giza
case_against.text: The rival location inside the same alternative tradition is the Hall of Records, held to lie under Giza. It is the far better known of the two claims and the one most people in this field mean when they talk about a hidden archive. The corpus carries no case for it. Nothing is supplied about who first placed the Hall at Giza, what they based it on, or what has been found there. The Giza position appears in this dispute as the well-known theory and nothing more, so on the material at hand it is named rather than argued.

disputes.claim: A tension exists between the use of modern scientific methods (ground-penetrating radar) to rediscover a lost structure and the alleged use of official authority to suppress and conceal the results of that discovery.

case_for.heading: Found by radar, then buried by authority
case_for.text: The claim has two halves and the corpus supports one of them. The expedition used ground penetrating radar, so the rediscovery was done by instrument rather than by rumour. Radar returns are a record. Someone ran the survey, and the survey produced results. That is the documented half. The second half, that official authority was then used to suppress and conceal those results, has nothing behind it in the corpus. No official is named. No order, refusal, or retraction is described. There is no account of who saw the data and what they did about it. As it stands the case rests on a single supplied fact about the method, with the accusation of concealment resting on nothing supplied at all.

case_against.heading: No case supplied on the other side
case_against.text: Nothing in the corpus argues the other way. No one from the archaeological authorities responds to the accusation. No alternative account of what happened to the radar results is offered, and there is no reading of the data from anyone who disputes what the expedition took it to show. Whatever answer exists, the corpus does not carry it.

disputes.claim: There is a tension between historical accounts from centuries ago describing a visible and partially explorable ruin and the current reality where the same site is completely buried, underwater, and its existence is not officially acknowledged.

case_for.heading: They walked into it once
case_for.text: The contrast is the argument. Centuries ago, people wrote about this site as something you could go and see. Parts of it were standing and parts of it could be walked through, and visitors put that on the record. Today the same place is under earth and under water, and its existence is not officially acknowledged. A ruin that was once described from the inside is now a site that is formally not there. On this side, that shift is the thing that needs explaining. The corpus supplies no detail to work with. No visitor is named and no account is quoted. There is no date for when the site went under, no measurement of the water, and no statement from any authority declining to acknowledge it. The shape of the contrast is given and the specifics are not.

case_against.heading: No case supplied on the other side
case_against.text: The corpus carries nothing against this. No one questions whether the old accounts describe the site people think they describe. No one offers an ordinary explanation for the burial or the water, such as a shifting river or a rising water table. And no one on the official side is quoted explaining why the site goes unacknowledged. The counter-case is absent rather than weak.

anecdotes.text: A full-time stenographer was retained to record Cayce's predictions because enough came true during his lifetime.
anecdotes.context: Cayce had gained a significant following due to the unexpected accuracy of his psychic readings over the years. Hiring a dedicated stenographer ensured that every statement was meticulously documented for future study and validation. This decision transformed his informal sessions into an extensive, permanently archived collection of prophecies.

anecdotes.text: Petrie became trapped in a collapsing tunnel and was freed after a worker tossed a lit match to help him orient himself and twist free.
anecdotes.context: Excavation work in unstable ruins frequently exposed archaeologists to sudden structural collapses. The brief flash of illumination provided just enough visual clarity for Petrie to assess his physical alignment and maneuver out of the debris. The incident highlighted the constant physical perils surrounding early field excavations.

anecdotes.text: The video is hosted by Johanna, who describes herself as an 'ancient technology hunter' making videos about ancient history.
anecdotes.context: Johanna produces digital content focused on re-evaluating historical sites and physical artifacts. Her platform leverages informal, accessible media to introduce alternative historical interpretations to a broader online audience. This approach establishes a public brand centered on exploring non-traditional archaeological theories.

anecdotes.text: Johanna recommends the book 'From Light Into Darkness' by Stephen Mehler, a colleague of Christopher Dunn, which records indigenous oral histories from Abd'El Hakim Awyan's father, one of the last wisdom keepers from the Khemitian (Chesan) people in Egypt.
anecdotes.context: Stephen Mehler's work seeks to preserve alternative historical narratives through regional oral traditions. By citing Abd'El Hakim Awyan, the text attempts to anchor alternative history concepts in local lineage and historical memory.

anecdotes.text: Johanna visited Hawara the year before her trip with Ben from Uncharted X and Jimmy from Bright Insight, but did not film there because she had COVID-19 at the time without realizing it.
anecdotes.context: An unexpected bout with illness altered her original research itinerary and postponed on-site documentation efforts. Her initial inability to record the location set up a necessary return trip alongside fellow content creators to gather footage. This delay shaped the production timeline for her eventual collaborative visual releases.

anecdotes.text: By the time of Lucas's visit, the passages he described could no longer be traced, having become blocked by debris.
anecdotes.context: Physical degradation and natural shifts over time frequently obscured previously mapped underground routes. Lucas's earlier written accounts remain critical because later researchers lost direct physical access to the subterranean layout. The accumulation of obstruction effectively shut off further direct investigation of those specific subterranean areas.

anecdotes.context: A. D. Scholars frequently utilize this specific edition to evaluate Herodotus's geographical and historical descriptions. Its structured format serves as a primary textual source across academic and digital research platforms.

anecdotes.context: Financial backing from educational initiatives enabled the large-scale digitization of foundational historical literature. Integrating classical works into the Perseus Digital Library made previously scarce texts immediately searchable for worldwide researchers. This effort accelerated the transition of classical humanities research into digital formats.

anecdotes.context: Applying this specific open license permits broad academic and educational redistribution without paywalls. It guarantees that subsequent users can freely adapt and distribute the material provided proper attribution is maintained. Requiring structural changes to be shared back protects the integrity of the centralized open-source repository. This mechanism ensures that community-driven corrections directly enhance the main digital collection.

anecdotes.text: The document mentions the places Hawara, Egypt; Ephesus, Turkey; and the City of Crocodiles, Egypt.
anecdotes.context: The narrative explicitly links these three geographical sites through historical connections and regional importance. Identifying these specific locations anchors the text's travel accounts and administrative descriptions to physical geography. The spatial framework allows researchers to map out classical travel routes and regional historical centers.

anecdotes.text: The page has five cross-references to other works, including Raphael Kühner and Bernhard Gerth's Ausführliche Grammatik der griechischen Sprache (sections 1.3.1 and 3.6.1).
anecdotes.context: Grammatical cross-references connect the primary source text directly to standard classical philology reference tools. Linking to Kühner and Gerth allows readers to analyze specific linguistic structures and nuances present in the original Greek. This structural integration supports rigorous textual analysis and accurate translation work.

anecdotes.text: The page is cross-referenced in Harper's dictionary under the entry 'Labyrinthus'.
anecdotes.context: Harper's dictionary provides essential context regarding classical concepts, architectural structures, and historical sites. Indexing the page under 'Labyrinthus' connects the specific source passage to broader historical discussions of complex ancient structures. This cross-reference assists scholars in comparing historical descriptions of labyrinths across different ancient authorities.

anecdotes.text: The page is cross-referenced in A Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities (1890) under the entry 'LABYRINTHUS'.
anecdotes.context: This 1890 reference volume serves as an authoritative guide on classical archaeological terms and material culture. Linking to the entry offers critical background on how nineteenth-century scholars interpreted ancient labyrinth constructions. It bridges primary historical narrative with formal classical archaeology research.

anecdotes.text: The page is cross-referenced in the Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography (1854) under the entry 'MOERIS LACUS'.
anecdotes.context: The entry in this 1854 reference work clarifies regional topography surrounding the artificial lake described by ancient historians. Linking the page to 'MOERIS LACUS' integrates textual accounts with historical geographical mapping of the Fayum basin. This connection helps researchers evaluate ancient claims regarding large-scale Egyptian hydraulic engineering.

anecdotes.text: The page has 25 cross-references in general dictionaries, including entries from the LSJ (Liddell-Scott-Jones) Greek lexicon.
anecdotes.context: Extensive integration with lexical resources helps readers unpack precise word choices and obscure terms in the original text. The LSJ lexicon provides definitive context regarding ancient Greek definitions, dialects, and technical terminology. These linked references significantly lower the barrier for detailed, line-by-line linguistic analysis.

anecdotes.text: One of the LSJ cross-reference entries is for the Greek word 'λα^βύρινθ-ος' (labyrinthos, meaning labyrinth).
anecdotes.context: This specific lexical entry defines the foundational Greek term used to describe massive, complex structural layouts. Linking the source text directly to this definition helps clarify whether the original author meant a figurative maze or a physical structure. It anchors historical debates about the famous Egyptian labyrinth in original language analysis.

anecdotes.text: Another LSJ cross-reference entry is for the Greek word 'τεσσα^ρα^κοντ-όργυιος', a term denoting a measurement of forty orguiai (fathoms).
anecdotes.context: The specialized measurement term defines exact physical dimensions stated within classical descriptions. Connecting the text to this specific unit of fathom-based length helps modern researchers calculate the precise scale intended by the ancient author. Accurate translation of these technical measurements prevents systemic errors in mapping structural footprints.

anecdotes.text: One commenter questions whether Hawara is the correct location, noting a pyramid image resembling one found by a Google Earth armchair archaeologist.
anecdotes.context: Disagreements over geographical locations highlight the friction between traditional archaeological identification and informal digital research. Relying on satellite imagery offers alternative candidates for ancient sites, challenging long-standing academic consensus. The exchange illustrates how public internet commentary actively debates established geographical placements.

anecdotes.text: Sean Rigby, the article's cited researcher, Professor of Chemical Engineering at the University of Nottingham, researches ancient glass manufacture and holds MAs in Ancient History and Ancient Religions from the University of Wales Trinity Saint David.
anecdotes.context: Professor Rigby's interdisciplinary background combines modern materials science with ancient historical context. His expertise in chemical analysis allows him to evaluate historical manufacturing techniques through a physical science perspective. This dual qualification enables sophisticated research into the technological capabilities of ancient industrial processes.

anecdotes.text: This buried Nile branch is 40 miles long and now hidden under the Sahara desert.
anecdotes.context: Satellites and modern radar imaging helped geologists map this ancient waterway beneath layers of sediment and arid landscape. Its proximity to several major archaeological sites suggests the region was once far greener and more hydrologically active. Identifying its full trajectory rewrites our understanding of how the ancient Egyptian geography evolved over millennia.

anecdotes.text: The discovery of the buried Nile branch could explain how ancient Egyptians transported massive stone blocks for pyramid construction.
anecdotes.context: For centuries, historians debated how megaton limestone and granite slabs were moved across vast desert stretches without modern machinery. A navigable waterway running directly past major monument sites provides a clear waterborne transit corridor for heavy cargo. This physical link solves a foundational logistical puzzle of ancient civil engineering.

anecdotes.text: Dr. Carmen Boulter previously created the docu-series The Pyramid Code.
anecdotes.context: Her earlier media work focused on alternative theories regarding ancient Egyptian technology, consciousness, and architectural origins. Building a public presence through television allowed her to popularize unconventional fringe perspectives on the purpose of monument sites. This background shaped her subsequent research directions and public commentary on Nile discoveries.

anecdotes.text: Khufu's Solar Boat was disassembled piece by piece and stored in dry desert sand at Giza, preserving it as one of the earliest organic artifacts on Earth.
anecdotes.context: Excavated in the mid-twentieth century, the cedar vessel was designed to carry the pharaoh through the afterlife alongside the sun god Ra. Its deliberate placement in an airtight stone pit prevented wood rot and decay for over four thousand years. Reconstructing the vessel provided invaluable insights into ancient shipwright techniques and ritual burial customs.

info_gaps.question: The sources repeatedly state that scans from 2008 and later found a huge underground structure. However, the actual scan images, data plots, or the official scientific reports from those expeditions are not included. You're relying on other people's descriptions of the evidence, not the evidence itself.
info_gaps.why: When a scientific claim is made based on technical data like ground-penetrating radar, the data itself is the primary evidence. To properly evaluate the claims, you need to see the data that led to the conclusions.
info_gaps.go_get: Search for the original Mataha Expedition report, which was reportedly published online, or any published papers or conference proceedings from the teams involved (Mataha, Merlin Burrows, Timothy Akers).

info_gaps.question: Multiple sources accuse former Egyptian official Zahi Hawass of actively suppressing the 2008 Mataha expedition findings. However, none of the sources provide a direct quote or statement from Hawass specifically addressing the Mataha expedition or the reasons for its alleged suppression. You have the accusation, but not his side of that specific story.
info_gaps.why: In any story involving serious accusations like scientific suppression, narrative balance requires seeking a response from the accused party. Their explanation or denial is a critical part of the story.
info_gaps.go_get: Search for interviews, press releases, or official statements from Zahi Hawass or the Supreme Council of Antiquities from the 2008-2010 period that mention the Hawara site or the Mataha expedition.

info_gaps.question: The sources claim the 2008 Mataha expedition team members were threatened and forced into non-disclosure. However, there are no direct, firsthand interviews or written accounts from those specific team members describing what happened to them.
